entry.title: ATUL Architecture #5 — Designing a Utility Data Fabric on SAP BTP
entry.content:
ATUL Architecture #5 — Designing a Utility Data Fabric on SAP BTP

How Utilities Build a Unified, Governed, Real‑Time Data Layer for Grid + Customer Operations

1.      Introduction

For SAP-centric utilities, the challenge is no longer simply managing growing volumes of data. Utilities have invested heavily in SAP IS-U, SAP S/4HANA, AMI platforms, SCADA systems, GIS applications, outage management solutions, and a growing ecosystem of grid technologies. Yet much of this information remains trapped within operational silos, making it difficult to create a unified view of grid and customer operations.

The real problem is no longer collecting data, but connecting, governing, and using it across the enterprise.

As utilities navigate the rise of distributed energy resources (DERs), electric vehicles (EVs), advanced metering infrastructure (AMI), and increasingly dynamic grid operations, traditional batch-oriented architectures struggle to keep pace. The grid is becoming real time, but the data architecture often remains fragmented.

A Business Data Fabric built on SAP Datasphere and SAP HANA Cloud provides a modern architectural approach for unifying SAP and non-SAP data without discarding existing investments. By combining data integration, semantic modeling, governance, and real-time access capabilities, utilities can create a trusted enterprise data layer that supports analytics, AI, operational intelligence, and regulatory reporting from a common foundation.

This is where Utility Data Fabric becomes essential—and where SAP BTP provides the platform to make it practical.

Most utilities still operate with:

  • Siloed operational systems
  • Fragmented data marts
  • Batch‑driven ETL pipelines
  • Inconsistent semantic definitions
  • Limited real‑time visibility

This creates a fundamental gap: The grid is real‑time, but the data architecture is not.

This is where Utility Data Fabric becomes essential — and SAP BTP provides the platform to build it.

2.      A Utility Data Fabric in Action: Transformer Outage Scenario

To understand how Utility Data Fabric works, consider a common operational event transformer failure affecting several hundred customers.

A SCADA system detects abnormal voltage conditions and reports the event in real time. AMI smart meters simultaneously stop communicating, confirming the outage footprint. GIS identifies the affected transformer, feeder, and service territory, while the Outage Management System (OMS) creates an outage event and initiates restoration activities.

Within the Utility Data Fabric, these events are combined with asset history, maintenance records, weather conditions, and customer information to create a unified operational view. Customer notification systems can automatically communicate outage information, analytics platforms can assess business impact, and AI models can predict restoration timelines based on historical outage patterns.

This single event touches nearly every layer of the Data Fabric—from data ingestion and semantic modeling to governance, analytics, and AI-driven decision support.

3.      What Utility Data Fabric Actually Means

Data Fabric is not a single product. It is an architectural approach that unifies:

  • Data ingestion
  • Data storage
  • Semantic modeling
  • Governance
  • Access control
  • Analytics
  • AI/ML consumption

Across all utility domains:

  • Grid operations
  • Customer operations
  • Metering
  • Billing
  • Asset management
  • Field operations
  • Regulatory reporting

In simple terms: A Data Fabric makes data findable, usable, trusted, and real‑time — across the entire utility.

SAP BTP provides the building blocks to make this practical.

4.      The Core Components of a Utility Data Fabric on SAP BTP

Data Lake Layer

This is the foundation. SAP HANA Cloud provides the underlying multi-model data platform for storing and processing enterprise data, while SAP Datasphere delivers the semantic, integration, and governance capabilities that form the Business Data Fabric layer. A key principle of SAP's Business Data Fabric approach is that not all data must be physically moved into a central repository. SAP Datasphere supports both replication and federation techniques, allowing utilities to access and combine data across SAP and non-SAP systems while minimizing unnecessary data duplication. This approach helps reduce integration costs, improve data freshness, and preserve investments in existing operational platforms. For large historical datasets such as AMI interval reads and telemetry archives, SAP HANA Cloud Data Lake can provide lower-cost storage while maintaining integration with Datasphere and HANA Cloud analytics services. In the transformer outage scenario, telemetry from SCADA, outage events from OMS, AMI meter status, GIS network topology, and customer information are ingested and made available through the Data Fabric for unified analysis

The Data Fabric approach allows utilities to federate data across hybrid landscapes—keeping legacy data in on-premises systems while virtualizing access in the cloud—reducing the latency and cost of moving massive, static datasets.

Utilities ingest:

  • AMI meter events
  • SCADA/IoT streams
  • DER telemetry
  • Weather + Wildfire Risk Data
  • Customer interactions
  • Billing determinants
  • Asset health and maintenance history
  • Outage management events (OMS)

For utilities, geospatial information is as important as transactional data. Modern Data Fabrics must integrate GIS systems, network topology models, feeder maps, outage polygons, vegetation management zones, and wildfire risk areas. By combining spatial context with customer, asset, and operational data, utilities can perform advanced use cases such as outage impact analysis, restoration prioritization, vegetation risk assessment, DER hosting capacity planning, and climate resilience modeling. SAP Datasphere can combine this geospatial context with operational and customer data to create business-ready models for planning, analytics, and AI use cases.

  • The data lake must support:
  • High‑volume ingestion
  • Low‑cost storage
  • Real‑time streaming
  • Time‑series analytics
  • Geospatial analysis

This is where grid + customer data finally live together.

Analytical Model and Consumption Model concepts in Datasphere. In SAP Datasphere, analytical models define measures and semantics, while consumption models expose business‑ready views for analytics and AI. The goal is not to move every dataset into one database. The goal is to provide one trusted view of enterprise data regardless of where it physically resides

Semantic Models

This is the most misunderstood part of a Data Fabric.

Semantic models define:

  • What is a meter?
  • What is an outage?
  • What is a transformer?
  • What is billing determinant?
  • What is a customer event?

Without semantic consistency:

  • Analytics break
  • AI models fail
  • Reports contradict each other
  • Regulatory submissions become risky

A Business Data Fabric combines data integration, governance, semantic modeling, and real-time access into a single enterprise architecture without requiring all data to be physically centralized. SAP Datasphere’s Business Data Fabric capabilities allow utilities to create:

  • Harmonized data models
  • Domain‑specific views
  • Reusable data products
  • Cross‑domain relationships.

Rather than exposing raw tables or application-specific structures, utilities can publish governed data products that package data with business meaning, ownership, quality standards, and access controls. Examples include a customer 360 product, Asset Health product, Outage Operations product, DER Portfolio product, or Transformer Risk product. These reusable data products become the primary mechanism through which analytics teams, AI solutions, operational applications, and business users consume trusted enterprise data. For example, during a transformer outage, different systems may refer to the same asset using different identifiers. Semantic models help establish a consistent definition of transformers, feeders, outages, and affected customers across all participating systems.

Master Data Foundation

Semantic consistency begins with trusted master data. Utilities often maintain customer, asset, feeder, transformer, meter, and service point information across multiple systems, including SAP S/4HANA, SAP IS-U, GIS platforms, outage management systems, and third-party applications.

Utility Data Fabric must establish a consistent master data foundation so that the same business object is represented identically across the enterprise. Without master data harmonization, analytics become unreliable, AI models generate inconsistent results, and cross-domain reporting loses credibility.

By combining semantic models with governed master data, utilities create a trusted foundation for enterprise-wide analytics, operational intelligence, and regulatory reporting. SAP Master Data Governance (MDG) can further support this foundation by governing critical utility master data domains and synchronizing trust records across enterprise applications.

Governance Layer

Governance is not documentation. It is control + trust: Utilities must define

  • Data ownership (domain‑driven)
  • Data quality rules
  • Lineage and traceability
  • Access policies
  • Retention and compliance
  • Security and privacy

SAP BTP provides:

  • Central governance via Datasphere
  • Cataloging and lineage
  • Role‑based access
  • Policy enforcement
  • Auditability

Governance is what makes Data Fabric safe. Utility Data Fabrics must also address cybersecurity and regulatory requirements. As operational technology (OT) data from AMI, SCADA, and grid systems becomes integrated with enterprise IT platforms, utilities must enforce appropriate segmentation, access controls, auditability, and compliance requirements such as NERC CIP where applicable. During an outage investigation, data lineage and auditability help utilities understand where information originated, how it was transformed, and whether operational decisions were based on trusted data sources.

Active Metadata: The Intelligence Behind the Data Fabric

A modern Data Fabric does not operate solely on data; it also depends on metadata that describes how data is created, transformed, consumed, and governed. Active metadata captures information such as data lineage, ownership, quality scores, usage patterns, business definitions, and relationships between datasets.

Within SAP Datasphere, metadata helps utilities understand where data originated, who owns it, how it is being used, and whether it meets governance standards. As utility data landscapes continue to grow, active metadata becomes essential for automated impact analysis, policy enforcement, data discovery, and trusted AI consumption.

In many successful Data Fabric implementations, metadata acts as the operational intelligence layer that continuously monitors and improves the health of the overall data ecosystem.

Analytics for Grid + Customer

This is where Data Fabric becomes valuable. Utilities can build:

Grid Analytics

  • Outage prediction
  • Load forecasting
  • DER hosting capacity
  • Feeder‑level performance
  • Voltage optimization
  • Asset failure prediction

Customer Analytics

  • High‑bill alerts
  • Usage pattern segmentation
  • EV charging behavior
  • Payment risk scoring
  • Real‑time notifications
  • Personalized rate recommendations

Enterprise Analytics

  • Regulatory reporting
  • Operational KPIs
  • Financial performance
  • Workforce optimization

SAP Analytics Cloud + Datasphere + HANA Cloud provide a unified analytics stack.

AI Readiness Through Data Fabric

The long-term value of a Utility Data Fabric extends beyond reporting and analytics. It provides the trusted data foundation required for enterprise AI, machine learning, and autonomous decision-making. AI models perform best when they are trained and operated on governed, semantically consistent, and high-quality data.

By combining semantic models, master data harmonization, governance controls, and lineage capabilities, a Utility Data Fabric reduces the risk of inaccurate predictions, inconsistent recommendations, and model drift. This foundation becomes critical for initiatives such as outage prediction, asset failure forecasting, energy demand optimization, and intelligent customer engagement. Examples include outage prediction, transformer failure forecasting, DER optimization, and proactive customer notification models. In the transformer outage example, AI models can combine outage history, asset condition, weather data, and crew availability to improve restoration estimates and recommend remediation actions.

BTP Integration:

This architecture doesn't exist in a vacuum. It integrates directly with SAP Build Process Automation (for triggering workflows from data insights) and SAP AI Core (for deploying models trained on Datasphere data products). SAP Integration Suite plays a critical role in Data Fabric architecture by connecting SAP IS-U, SAP S/4HANA, SAP EAM, GIS systems, outage management platforms, and external data providers. Through Cloud Integration, API Management, and Event Mesh, Integration Suite enables secure, governed, and scalable movement of data across hybrid utility landscapes.

How the Data Fabric Works End‑to‑End

Step 1 — Ingest

  • AMI events via Event Mesh
  • IoT/SCADA via MQTT
  • Customer interactions via APIs
  • Asset data via S/4HANA

Traditional data architectures rely on batch-based movement of information between systems. Modern utility operations require a different approach. Smart meters, distributed energy resources, grid sensors, and customer engagement platforms continuously generate events that must be processed in near real time. SAP Event Mesh enables these events to be distributed across operational systems and data platforms, where they can be consumed by analytics, automation services, and AI models. creating a continuously updated Data Fabric rather than a periodically refreshed repository.

Step 2 — Store

  • Raw zone (immutable)
  • Refined zone (cleaned)
  • Curated zone (business‑ready)

Step 3 — Model

  • Semantic definitions
  • Domain views
  • Data products

Step 4 — Govern

  • Quality rules
  • Lineage
  • Access control

Step 5 — Consume

  • Grid operations
  • Customer operations
  • Field mobility
  • AI/ML models
  • Analytics dashboards

This is the Utility Data Fabric lifecycle.  The Data Fabric helps align grid‑level latency requirements (millisecond responses for protection) with enterprise‑level latency (near real‑time analytics), ensuring the data architecture does not become a bottleneck for critical operations.

Returning to our transformer outage example, the same operational event moves through every stage of the Data Fabric lifecycle—from ingestion and storage through semantic modeling, governance, analytics, and AI-driven decision support.

5.       Why Utilities Need Data Fabric Now

  • Because the grid is becoming real‑time: DERs, EVs, and AMI require continuous intelligence.
  • Because AI depends on clean, governed data: AI is useless without trusted data.
  • Because regulators expect transparency: Lineage, auditability, and data quality are no longer optional.
  • Because customer expectations have changed: Real‑time notifications, usage insights, and personalized experiences require unified data.
  • Because operational silos are too expensive: A Data Fabric reduces duplication, integration cost, and data chaos.

6.      Data Fabric vs Traditional Utility Data Warehouse

Many utilities already operate enterprise data warehouses and may question why a Data Fabric is needed. Traditional data warehouses typically rely on periodic ETL processes that copy data into centralized repositories for reporting purposes. While effective for historical analytics, they often struggle to support real-time operational use cases, cross-domain intelligence, and AI-driven decision making.

Utility Data Fabric complements and extends the traditional warehouse by introducing semantic consistency, federated data access, active governance, reusable data products, and near real-time integration. Rather than simply storing data, the Data Fabric creates a governed and intelligent data layer that connects operational systems, analytical platforms, and AI services across the enterprise.

In simple terms, a traditional warehouse answers questions about the past, while a Data Fabric enables utilities to act on what is happening now.

Traditional Data Warehouse

  • Periodic ETL
  • Historical reporting
  • Centralized storage
  • Primarily analytics focused

Data Fabric

  • Real-time data access
  • Federation and virtualization
  • Semantic consistency
  • Data products
  • AI consumption
  • Cross-domain intelligence

7.      Common Pitfalls (What Fails in Real Projects):

Pitfall: Attempting to replicate all data instead of federating it. Leverage Datasphere’s ability to virtualize data from SAP S/4HANA and external sources to reduce ETL overhead and latency.

  • Treating the Data Fabric as an IT project: It must be business‑owned and domain‑driven.
  • Overloading the data lake with unstructured noise: Raw data without governance becomes a “data swamp.”
  • No semantic consistency: Different teams define the same metric differently.
  • Ignoring real‑time ingestion: Batch pipelines cannot support modern grid operations.
  • Not designing data products:  Data must be reusable, not one‑off.

The Architecture Principle That Matters Most

Data Fabric is not a database. It is a governed operating model for how utility data is shared, trusted, and consumed across the enterprise.

SAP BTP provides the platform.  The utility provides discipline.

What Success Looks Like

A successful Utility Data Fabric delivers:

  • A single source of truth
  • Real‑time grid + customer visibility
  • Faster regulatory reporting
  • Higher data quality
  • Better AI outcomes
  • Lower integration cost
  • Stronger cybersecurity posture
  • Improved customer experience

This is the foundation for the AI‑enabled utility.

8.      Executive Insight

Historically, utilities integrated applications.

The next generation utility will compete on the quality, trustworthiness, and usability of its data as much as the reliability of its physical infrastructure.

Organizations that establish trusted, governed, and reusable data products will be better positioned to deploy AI, automate operations, accelerate regulatory reporting, and improve customer experience. The competitive advantage will come not from possessing more data, but from creating a data architecture capable of turning data into operational intelligence.

9.      Final Thought

Utilities don’t need more data. They need better architecture for the data they already have.

A Utility Data Fabric on SAP BTP creates:

  • A unified data layer
  • A governed semantic foundation
  • A real‑time operational backbone
  • A scalable platform for AI and analytics

In the next decade, utilities that master their data will lead. Those that don’t will struggle with reliability, cost, and customer expectations.

Next in the Series — ATUL Architecture #6

We move into the intelligence layer:

  • AI‑driven grid operations
  • Predictive models for BTP
  • Real‑time decision engines
  • Digital twins
  • Autonomous workflows

This is where Data Fabric becomes the brain of the modern utility.

entry.title: Calling ABAP RFC Function Modules from SAP BTP Kyma with SAP Java Connector
entry.content:
Why I Wrote This

I recently wanted to build a small demo application that proves a simple point:

Can an application running on SAP BTP Kyma call an on-premise SAP system via RFC?

At first glance, this sounds like something that should be straightforward. SAP Java Connector exists, SAP Cloud Connector exists, Kyma has Connectivity Proxy, and SAP BTP has Destination service. Surely we just package sapjco3.jar, create a destination, and call STFC_CONNECTION, right?

Well — almost, but not quite.

While researching this, I found SAP Community questions such as “How can I connect my SAP BTP Kyma with my On-Premise system (ECC6 EHP7) via RFC”. The discussion captures the same uncertainty I ran into: Cloud Foundry examples exist, but Kyma is different because we build and run our own container images. There is no magic “built JCo” unless we explicitly bring the right runtime pieces (I was happy to see my own github repo referenced in the question - another indication that there is nothing out there for RFC and Kyma).

This blog documents the working path I ended up with.

Note: This is a proof of concept - SAP is not (yet) supporting this scenario. If that changes I will update the blog. 

The Goal

The goal was intentionally small:

  • Run a Java application in SAP BTP Kyma.
  • Resolve an RFC destination from SAP BTP Destination service.
  • Route RFC traffic through Kyma Connectivity Proxy.
  • Reach an on-premise SAP S/4HANA system via SAP Cloud Connector.
  • Execute STFC_CONNECTION.

The successful response looked like this:

{
  "ok": true,
  "destination": "InsightSuiteDestination",
  "function": "STFC_CONNECTION",
  "jcoVersion": "3.1.13.2 (2026-04-22) for SAP Business Technology Platform",
  "exports": {
    "ECHOTEXT": "Hello from Kyma",
    "RESPTEXT": "SAP R/3 Rel. 816   Sysid: S4H ... Logon_Data: 201/RFC_TESTUSER/E"
  }
}

That was the happy end. The rest of this post is about how to get there.

High-Level Architecture

The final request flow is:

HTTP client
  -> Kyma Istio route
  -> Java/Tomcat app in Kyma
  -> SAP JCo cloud runtime
  -> SAP BTP Destination service
  -> Kyma Connectivity Proxy RFC port 20001
  -> SAP Cloud Connector
  -> on-premise SAP system RFC gateway
  -> STFC_CONNECTION

For this demo, the relevant names were:

Kyma namespace:        jco-rfc-test
RFC destination:       InsightSuiteDestination
Cloud Connector ID:    sap-insight-suite
Virtual RFC host:      s4hana-2025japan
System number:         00
SAP client:            201
RFC function:          STFC_CONNECTION

Key Lesson 1: Plain JCo Is Not Enough

My first attempt was the obvious one: package SAP JCo into a Tomcat image and run a servlet.

That was enough to start the app, but not enough to make the BTP/Kyma on-premise path work. The plain runtime did not know how to resolve BTP destinations and route RFC through the Kyma Connectivity Proxy with the required proxy authorization.

The working setup needed the SAP JCo cloud/connectivity runtime libraries that are normally provided by SAP Java Buildpack.

The important runtime ingredients were:

com.sap.conn.jco.cloud-3.1.13.2.jar
com.sap.conn.jco.cloud.rt.cloud-3.1.13.2.jar
com.sap.core.connectivity.jco-5.0.7.jar
com.sap.core.connectivity.jco.cf-5.0.7.jar
com.sap.core.connectivity.cloud.destinations.tunnel-0.9.267.jar

In my case these came from:

xs-java-buildpack-2.66.0-offline-cnb-tomcat.tgz

I used the buildpack archive as a runtime overlay and copied its Tomcat libraries into my image. If you have access to the official builder, using pack build is the cleaner path.

The Minimal Java Code

The Java code itself is pleasantly small. The servlet resolves a destination and calls a function module:

JCoDestination destination = JCoDestinationManager.getDestination("InsightSuiteDestination");
JCoFunction function = destination.getRepository().getFunction("STFC_CONNECTION");

function.getImportParameterList().setValue("REQUTEXT", "Hello from Kyma");
function.execute(destination);

String echoText = function.getExportParameterList().getString("ECHOTEXT");
String responseText = function.getExportParameterList().getString("RESPTEXT");

The demo app exposes this through an HTTP endpoint:

/rfc?destination=InsightSuiteDestination&text=Hello%20from%20Kyma

Build Setup

The app is a WAR file running on Java 17 and Tomcat 10.1.

One important detail: SAP Java Buildpack 2.x uses the Jakarta servlet stack, so the application uses jakarta.servlet.*, not javax.servlet.*.

Relevant Maven setup:

<packaging>war</packaging>

<properties>
  <maven.compiler.release>17</maven.compiler.release>
</properties>

<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>com.sap.conn.jco</groupId>
    <artifactId>sapjco3</artifactId>
    <version>3.1.13</version>
    <scope>system</scope>
    <systemPath>${project.basedir}/lib/sapjco3.jar</systemPath>
  </dependency>

  <dependency>
    <groupId>jakarta.servlet</groupId>
    <artifactId>jakarta.servlet-api</artifactId>
    <version>6.1.0</version>
    <scope>provided</scope>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

Container Image

The working image used Tomcat 10.1 and copied the SAP buildpack runtime overlay:

FROM docker.io/library/maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-17 AS build
WORKDIR /workspace
COPY pom.xml ./
COPY lib ./lib
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn -q -DskipTests package

FROM docker.io/library/tomcat:10.1-jre17-temurin
ENV LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/usr/local/tomcat/impl/linuxx86_64:/usr/local/tomcat/lib \
    JAVA_OPTS="-Djava.library.path=/usr/local/tomcat/impl/linuxx86_64:/usr/local/tomcat/lib"

COPY .tmp-buildpack/tomcat/bin/ /usr/local/tomcat/bin/
COPY .tmp-buildpack/tomcat/conf/ /usr/local/tomcat/conf/
COPY .tmp-buildpack/tomcat/lib/ /usr/local/tomcat/lib/
COPY .tmp-buildpack/tomcat/impl/ /usr/local/tomcat/impl/
COPY --from=build /workspace/target/jco-on-kyma-demo.war /usr/local/tomcat/webapps/ROOT.war
EXPOSE 8080

Before building, extract the buildpack archive:

mkdir -p .tmp-buildpack/tomcat
tar -xzf java-buildpack/xs-java-buildpack-2.66.0-offline-cnb-tomcat.tgz \
  -C .tmp-buildpack/tomcat

Then build and push the image to a registry Kyma can pull from.

Kyma Service Bindings

The application needs at least:

  • Destination service instance and binding
  • XSUAA service instance and binding
  • Connectivity Proxy config and secret available in the application namespace

Example BTP service resources:

apiVersion: services.cloud.sap.com/v1
kind: ServiceInstance
metadata:
  name: destination-jco
  namespace: jco-rfc-test
spec:
  serviceOfferingName: destination
  servicePlanName: lite
---
apiVersion: services.cloud.sap.com/v1
kind: ServiceBinding
metadata:
  name: destination-jco
  namespace: jco-rfc-test
spec:
  serviceInstanceName: destination-jco
---
apiVersion: services.cloud.sap.com/v1
kind: ServiceInstance
metadata:
  name: xsuaa-jco
  namespace: jco-rfc-test
spec:
  serviceOfferingName: xsuaa
  servicePlanName: application
---
apiVersion: services.cloud.sap.com/v1
kind: ServiceBinding
metadata:
  name: xsuaa-jco
  namespace: jco-rfc-test
spec:
  serviceInstanceName: xsuaa-jco

The SAP runtime expected the bindings as files. Injecting them only as environment variables was not sufficient in my setup.

- name: SERVICE_BINDING_ROOT
  value: "/etc/secrets/sapbtp"

And mount the binding secrets:

volumeMounts:
  - name: destination-binding
    mountPath: /etc/secrets/sapbtp/destination-jco
    readOnly: true
  - name: xsuaa-binding
    mountPath: /etc/secrets/sapbtp/xsuaa-jco
    readOnly: true

volumes:
  - name: destination-binding
    secret:
      secretName: destination-jco
  - name: xsuaa-binding
    secret:
      secretName: xsuaa-jco

Connectivity Proxy Environment

For RFC, the app uses Connectivity Proxy port 20001:

- name: ONPREMISE_PROXY_HOST
  valueFrom:
    configMapKeyRef:
      name: connectivity-proxy-info
      key: onpremise_proxy_host
- name: ONPREMISE_PROXY_RFC_PORT
  valueFrom:
    configMapKeyRef:
      name: connectivity-proxy-info
      key: onpremise_proxy_rfc_port
- name: ONPREMISE_PROXY_TENANT_MODE
  valueFrom:
    configMapKeyRef:
      name: connectivity-proxy-info
      key: onpremise_proxy_tenant_mode
- name: CP_SECRET_CONNECTIVITY_PROXY_KYMA_SYSTEM
  valueFrom:
    secretKeyRef:
      name: cp-secret-connectivity-proxy-kyma-system
      key: service_key

In this demo the proxy endpoint was:

connectivity-proxy.kyma-system.svc.cluster.local:20001

Creating the RFC Destination

This part is easy to miss.

The RFC destination is not a Kubernetes Destination custom resource. For this JCo flow, the destination must exist in SAP BTP Destination service, and JCo resolves it from there.

The working destination properties were:

Name=InsightSuiteDestination
Type=RFC
jco.client.ashost=s4hana-2025japan
jco.client.sysnr=00
jco.client.client=201
jco.client.user=RFC_TESTUSER
jco.client.passwd=<password>
jco.client.lang=EN
jco.destination.proxy_type=OnPremise
jco.client.cloud_connector_location_id=sap-insight-suite

The most important line for the Location ID was:

jco.client.cloud_connector_location_id=sap-insight-suite

Initially, I used only:

CloudConnectorLocationId=sap-insight-suite

That appeared as a raw/custom property but did not populate the RFC destination's Location ID field in SAP BTP Cockpit. The tunnel was opened as if the location ID was empty.

After adding jco.client.cloud_connector_location_id, Cockpit showed the Location ID correctly, and Connectivity Proxy opened the expected tunnel:

account:///.../sap-insight-suite

In the repository I created a small helper script to create the destination through the Destination service API:

export RFC_PASSWORD='<password>'

./scripts/upsert-rfc-destination.py \
  --namespace jco-rfc-test \
  --binding-secret destination-jco \
  --template destinations/InsightSuiteDestination.template.json \
  --delete-first

unset RFC_PASSWORD

Connectivity Proxy Authorization

Another issue I hit was proxy authorization. The Connectivity Proxy log showed:

Validation of token failed due to: Allowed client ids not set for region configuration id default

The fix was to configure the allowed client ID in the ConnectivityProxy custom resource:

CLIENTID=$(kubectl -n kyma-system get secret cp-secret-connectivity-proxy-kyma-system \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.service_key}' \
  | base64 -d \
  | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)["clientid"])')

python3 - <<PY > /tmp/cp-patch.json
import json
clientid = "$CLIENTID"
print(json.dumps({
  "spec": {
    "config": {
      "servers": {
        "proxy": {
          "authorization": {
            "oauth": {
              "allowedClientId": clientid
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}))
PY

kubectl -n kyma-system patch connectivityproxy connectivity-proxy \
  --type merge \
  --patch-file /tmp/cp-patch.json

After this, the proxy accepted the token and opened the RFC tunnel.

How to Recognize Success

Application logs showed:

Connected to socket with {sap-insight-suite-RFC.connectivity,2}
RfcOpen(... SCCLOCATIONID=sap-insight-suite)=1
Executing function STFC_CONNECTION

Connectivity Proxy logs showed:

Will use tunnelId: account:///.../sap-insight-suite
Handshake with tunnel client completed successfully

And the endpoint returned:

{
  "ok": true,
  "exports": {
    "ECHOTEXT": "Hello from Kyma"
  }
}

Things I Would Watch Out For

Here are the stumbling blocks that cost the most time:

  1. Plain JCo is not enough
    You need the SAP JCo cloud/connectivity runtime, not only sapjco3.jar and libsapjco3.so.

  2. SAP Java Buildpack 2.x means Jakarta
    If you use the 2.x runtime libraries, use Java 17 and jakarta.servlet.*.

  3. Mount service bindings as files
    The runtime looked for service bindings under /etc/secrets/sapbtp.

  4. Use the RFC-specific Location ID property
    For RFC destinations, use jco.client.cloud_connector_location_id.

  5. Connectivity Proxy may need allowed client ID configuration
    If you see Allowed client ids not set, patch the ConnectivityProxy configuration.

  6. Reduce debug logging after troubleshooting
    JCo/connectivity debug logs can expose destination details and token payloads.

Final Thoughts

Once all pieces were in place, the actual RFC call was simple. The hard part was not the Java code; it was assembling the correct runtime and configuration around it.

The most important takeaway for me was this:

In Kyma, RFC via JCo is possible, but you need the SAP cloud JCo/connectivity runtime and a correctly maintained BTP RFC destination.

Hopefully this saves someone else a few debugging loops — especially around the Location ID and Connectivity Proxy authorization details.

Appendix: Minimal Checklist

  • [ ] Connectivity Proxy module is installed and RFC port 20001 is enabled.
  • [ ] SAP Cloud Connector is connected to the correct subaccount.
  • [ ] Cloud Connector exposes the virtual RFC host/system.
  • [ ] Destination service instance and binding exist in the app namespace.
  • [ ] XSUAA service instance and binding exist in the app namespace.
  • [ ] Service bindings are mounted under /etc/secrets/sapbtp.
  • [ ] App image includes SAP JCo cloud/connectivity runtime libraries.
  • [ ] RFC destination exists in BTP Destination service.
  • [ ] RFC destination has jco.client.cloud_connector_location_id if a Location ID is used.
  • [ ] Connectivity Proxy authorization allows the connectivity client ID.
  • [ ] STFC_CONNECTION works with the configured SAP user.

entry.title: Kyma on k3d, Revisited.
entry.content:
No Kyma trial. No drama — well, no Kyma at all, actually.

SAP pulled the Kyma runtime from the BTP trial a while back, no ETA on return. The free tier alternative doesn't fully solve it either: Kyma on the free tier is available once per global account, for up to 30 days — after that, it's gone unless you're paying. So if you're between a suspended trial and a free tier clock that's already run out, running Kyma locally on k3d fills the gap.

A while back I wrote about running Kyma locally on k3d as a workaround for the BTP trial's Kyma runtime being suspended (see "No Kyma Runtime? No Problem — Running Kyma Locally with k3d"). Recently I rebuilt that same setup from scratch on the same machine because I had absolutely no Kyma environments to use at all! A few things had moved on underneath it since — nothing about Kyma itself, just the ordinary drift you get from module versions, defaults, and environment differences changing over time. Here's what came up and how each was resolved.

Full repo: https://github.com/neilaspin/k3d

Starting Point: An Existing Cluster, and a KUBECONFIG Detail

Before building anything new, it's worth checking what's already there:

docker info
k3d cluster list

If there's an old cluster from a previous session, plain kubectl commands might not see it. In my case, kubectl config get-contexts came back empty for the k3d cluster — not because the cluster was gone, but because my shell profile permanently exports KUBECONFIG pointing at a downloaded BTP kubeconfig file. Worth checking:

grep -n "KUBECONFIG" ~/.zshrc ~/.zprofile ~/.zshenv

That override means plain kubectl never reads the default ~/.kube/config, which is where k3d writes its own cluster context. Rather than editing .zshrc, pointing at the right file explicitly works fine:

kubectl --kubeconfig ~/.kube/config config get-contexts
kubectl --kubeconfig ~/.kube/config config use-context k3d-kyma

Or for the whole session:

export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config

Deviation 1: APIRule v1beta1 Has Been Retired

Following the original steps, applying the APIRule failed:

Error from server (Forbidden): ... v1beta1 APIRule version is no longer supported, please use v2 instead

The original post's module install step pulls from the "latest" release channel by design, which means the APIRule schema in use will naturally track whatever API Gateway currently supports — and v1beta1 has since been retired in favour of v2. Worth checking the currently-installed CRD directly rather than assuming an older example still matches:

kubectl get crd apirules.gateway.kyma-project.io -o jsonpath='{.spec.versions[*].name}'
kubectl explain apirule.spec --api-version=gateway.kyma-project.io/v2

The schema change itself is small — host becomes a hosts list, and accessStrategies: [{handler: no_auth}] becomes a noAuth: true flag under the rule. Once rewritten to v2, the APIRule is accepted normally.

Deviation 2: The Function's Namespace Needs the Istio Label Too

With the APIRule accepted, the next issue was more subtle:

kubectl get apirule hello-kyma -n default -o yaml
Validation errors: ... Pod default/hello-kyma-... does not have an injected istio sidecar

The Istio module install step labels kyma-system for sidecar injection, but the function itself runs in default, which needs the same label for the ingress gateway to establish mTLS with it:

kubectl label namespace default istio-injection=enabled --overwrite
kubectl delete pod -n default -l serverless.kyma-project.io/function-name=hello-kyma

Once the new pod shows 2/2 containers ready, the sidecar is present and the APIRule can reconcile properly.

Deviation 3: HTTP Now Redirects to HTTPS by Default

With both of the above resolved, the APIRule reconciled to Ready:

kubectl annotate apirule hello-kyma -n default reconcile=$(date +%s) --overwrite
kubectl get apirule hello-kyma -n default -o jsonpath='{.status.state}{"\n"}{.status.description}'

→ Ready / Reconciled successfully

But the plain HTTP test came back as a redirect rather than the function's response:

curl -s -m 8 http://hello-kyma.local.kyma.dev:31080 -w "\nHTTP %{http_code}\n"

→ HTTP 301

Checking the Gateway resource explains why:

kubectl get gateway kyma-gateway -n kyma-system -o jsonpath='{.spec.servers}'
{"port":{"number":80,"protocol":"HTTP"},"tls":{"httpsRedirect":true}}

httpsRedirect: true on the HTTP server is the current Istio module default. Switching the test to HTTPS is the straightforward fix here.

Deviation 4: Non-Default Ports and Istio's Host Matching

Testing over HTTPS instead (https://hello-kyma.local.kyma.dev:31443) hit a further error — RBAC: access denied. Since this cluster was built on non-default host ports (31443 rather than 30443, to avoid clashing with another cluster already running), it was worth checking exactly how the AuthorizationPolicy matches the request. Looking at the function pod's own Envoy sidecar config:

header: { name: ":authority", string_match: { exact: "hello-kyma.local.kyma.dev" } }

Istio compiles the AuthorizationPolicy's host match as an exact string against the :authority (Host) header, port included if the request includes one. curl only omits the port from that header when it matches the URL scheme's default (80 for http, 443 for https) — so on a non-default port like 31443, curl sends hello-kyma.local.kyma.dev:31443, which doesn't exactly match the policy's hello-kyma.local.kyma.dev.

Confirmed by forcing the header manually:

curl -sk -H "Host: hello-kyma.local.kyma.dev" https://hello-kyma.local.kyma.dev:31443

→ Hello from local Kyma!
→ HTTP 200

Worth knowing if you're ever running Kyma on non-standard ports locally, alongside another cluster or for any other reason — Istio's host matching is stricter about ports than you might expect.

Summary

A few things needed adjusting compared to the original walkthrough — an APIRule schema update, a namespace label, and two defaults (HTTPS redirect, host-port matching) that don't come up unless you're on non-standard ports. None of them are Kyma issues as such; they're the normal effect of following a "latest"-pinned install against static example YAML some months on. Worth checking the current CRD schema, the Gateway's actual server config, and your port setup directly if something that "should" work doesn't — all four were quick fixes once identified.

Tested on macOS with k3d v5.8.3, k3s v1.33.6, kubectl v1.35.2, current ("latest" release channel) Kyma Istio and API Gateway modules.

entry.title: Calling the SAP Business Partner API from k3d: Bridging a Local Cluster to a Real BTP Subaccount
entry.content:
A separate post walked through calling the SAP Business Partner API from a Kyma Deployment on a managed cluster, using the BTP Service Operator to provision a Destination Service instance. Once I had a local Kyma-on-k3d setup running (see my "Kyma on k3d" posts), the obvious next question was whether the same thing runs entirely locally.

Context for why this matters: the BTP trial's Kyma environment has been suspended for a while, no ETA on return, and the free tier only gives you Kyma once per global account, for up to 30 days. Once that's gone, k3d is the only way to keep working with this pattern.

Short answer: mostly, except for one piece.

Why This Isn't a Pure Local Problem

The container, Deployment, Service, and Istio APIRule port over with zero changes — same as the earlier k3d posts.

Destination Service and XSUAA don't port over for free. They're not part of Kyma, they're BTP cloud services. A managed Kyma cluster comes with the BTP Service Operator pre-installed and already wired to your subaccount's Service Manager. A bare k3d cluster has none of that, and there's no offline stand-in for a real Destination Service.

The fix: install the BTP Service Operator into the local cluster and point it at a real BTP subaccount — the standard pattern for any self-managed Kubernetes cluster, Kyma or not.

Step 1: Check the Marketplace

cf marketplace

Look for service-manager and destination. Both need to be there — if service-manager isn't offered in your subaccount, stop here.

Step 2: Create a Service Manager Instance and Key

cf create-service service-manager subaccount-admin sm-k3d-operator
cf create-service-key sm-k3d-operator sm-k3d-operator-key
cf service-key sm-k3d-operator sm-k3d-operator-key

Use the subaccount-admin plan — SAP's own docs use it for this pattern, since the operator needs to provision services anywhere in the subaccount.

Output looks like this (redacted — treat this as a live credential, not something to commit anywhere):

{
  "credentials": {
    "clientid": "sb-<redacted>!b91247|service-manager!b37",
    "clientsecret": "<redacted>",
    "sm_url": "https://service-manager.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com",
    "uaadomain": "authentication.<region>.hana.ondemand.com",
    "url": "https://<subaccount>.authentication.<region>.hana.ondemand.com",
    "xsappname": "<redacted>"
  }
}

This is a real object in your actual subaccount — it survives a k3d cluster delete.

Step 3: Map Credentials to Helm Parameters

The sap-btp-operator chart's parameter names don't match the JSON fields above 1:1 — check the chart README rather than guessing:

  • clientid → manager.secret.clientid
  • clientsecret → manager.secret.clientsecret
  • sm_url → manager.secret.sm_url
  • url (the UAA one) → manager.secret.tokenurl

One gotcha: tokenurl wants the bare UAA URL, not the full /oauth/token path — the chart appends that itself via a separate tokenurlsuffix parameter. Include /oauth/token yourself and it doubles up.

helm repo add sap-btp-operator https://sap.github.io/sap-btp-service-operator
helm repo update

helm upgrade --install sap-btp-operator sap-btp-operator/sap-btp-operator \
  --create-namespace \
  --namespace sap-btp-operator \
  --kube-context k3d-kyma-local \
  --set manager.secret.clientid="<clientid>" \
  --set manager.secret.clientsecret="<clientsecret>" \
  --set manager.secret.sm_url="<sm_url>" \
  --set manager.secret.tokenurl="<url>"

Step 4: First Attempt Fails

Error: unable to build kubernetes objects from release manifest:
[resource mapping not found for name: "sap-btp-operator-serving-cert"
namespace: "sap-btp-operator" from "": no matches for kind "Certificate"
in version "cert-manager.io/v1"
ensure CRDs are installed first, resource mapping not found for name:
"sap-btp-operator-selfsigned-issuer" ... no matches for kind "Issuer"
in version "cert-manager.io/v1"
ensure CRDs are installed first]

The chart's webhook needs a TLS cert and expects cert-manager already installed to generate one. Managed Kyma clusters likely have it; a bare k3d cluster doesn't.

kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/latest/download/cert-manager.yaml

Wait for its three pods (cert-manager, cert-manager-cainjector, cert-manager-webhook) to reach Running, then retry the Helm command unchanged.

Step 5: Confirm It Landed

kubectl get pods -n sap-btp-operator
NAME                                                   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
sap-btp-operator-controller-manager-78fcf7b549-hxgqs   2/2     Running   0          22s
sap-btp-operator-controller-manager-78fcf7b549-ltnw2   2/2     Running   0          22s

Both replicas Running, 2/2. The operator's live in the local cluster, authenticated against the real subaccount from Step 2.

Key Points

The Service Operator bridges to real BTP regardless of where the cluster runs. Local k3d or managed Kyma, same credentials, same cloud dependency.

cert-manager is an undocumented prerequisite for this chart. Install it first on a bare cluster.

Use the subaccount-admin plan for the Service Manager instance, not a narrower one.

Helm parameter names don't match the JSON field names. Check the chart README — tokenurl specifically wants the bare UAA URL, not the full /oauth/token path.

Next: create the ServiceInstance/ServiceBinding for the destination service itself, and confirm it shows up as a real Destination Service instance in the BTP cockpit.

entry.title: Designing a Knowledge Base Article Search Agent Using SAP AI Solutions
entry.content:
Enterprise Document Discovery Powered by SAP Business AI, SAP AI Core, SAP HANA Cloud Vector Engine, and SAP BTP

Executive Summary

The Business Problem

Enterprise knowledge is rarely centralised. Across most SAP customer organisations, critical information is distributed across Microsoft SharePoint sites, Microsoft 365 repositories, shared network folders, PDF documents, Word files, Excel workbooks, PowerPoint decks, and internal knowledge bases. Subject matter experts hold process knowledge in personal drives. Project teams maintain functional design documents and technical specifications in disconnected locations. Support teams manage Knowledge Base Articles (KBAs) in systems that are not easily searchable across the broader organisation.

The consequence is predictable, users cannot find the right document at the right time. They raise support tickets for issues that have already been resolved. They duplicate effort because existing process documentation is not discoverable. They depend on colleagues ‘tribal knowledge’ rather than structured, reusable content.

Traditional keyword search compounds the problem. Keyword-based retrieval matches exact terms, not intent. A user searching for "payment run error" will not retrieve a document titled "FI period-end processing failure" even if the content is directly relevant. Keyword search does not understand synonyms, contextual meaning, or the relationship between a user's question and the substance of a document. It returns results based on word frequency, not relevance.

The Proposed Solution

This whitepaper proposes how customers and service providers can architect and build a Knowledge Base Article (KBA) Search Agent built on top of SAP AI solutions. The agent enables users to submit natural language queries and receive ranked, relevant documents drawn from across the enterprise content landscape, regardless of where those documents are stored or what format they are in.

The agent is not a reporting tool or an analytics dashboard. Its purpose is knowledge discovery: helping users find the most relevant document for their query, faster and with greater confidence.

The business value is direct:

  • Faster issue resolution: Users find relevant KBAs, process guides, and technical specifications without manual searching across multiple repositories.
  • Improved knowledge reuse: Existing documentation is surfaced and consumed rather than recreated.
  • Reduced dependency on tribal knowledge: Institutional knowledge becomes discoverable and accessible to all authorised users.
  • Better user productivity: Time spent searching is reduced; time spent resolving issues or completing tasks is increased.

SAP Joule, SAP's generative AI digital assistant, already demonstrates this model within SAP's own product portfolio, allowing employees to ask questions in plain language and receive answers grounded in business data. The KBA Search Agent extends this principle to enterprise document repositories.

Reference Architecture

Architecture Overview

The KBA Search Agent is built on a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture. RAG combines the retrieval of relevant documents from a vector store with the contextual understanding of a large language model (LLM), enabling the agent to return results that are grounded in actual enterprise content rather than generated from model memory alone.

The architecture operates as follows: a user submits a natural language query through the interaction layer. The query is converted into a vector embedding using an embedding model accessed via the SAP Generative AI Hub. That embedding is used to perform a similarity search against the SAP HANA Cloud Vector Engine, which stores pre-computed embeddings of all indexed enterprise documents. The most semantically similar document chunks are retrieved, ranked, and returned to the user with source references and relevance indicators.

 

 

Key Components

User Interaction Layer Users interact with the agent through SAP Joule or a custom interface built using SAP Build. SAP Joule supports natural language queries and runs within SAP BTP environments, requiring authentication between SAP Cloud Identity, SAP BTP, and the target system. SAP Build enables low-code construction of a dedicated search interface where users can submit queries, view ranked results, and navigate to source documents.

 

Agent Orchestration Layer SAP AI Core serves as the runtime for the agent's orchestration logic. It manages the embedding model, the retrieval pipeline, and the connection to the SAP HANA Cloud Vector Engine. The SAP Generative AI Hub, available within SAP AI Core, provides access to foundation models and LLMs for both embedding generation and, where appropriate, response synthesis. SAP AI Launchpad provides the management and monitoring interface for AI models, deployments, and prompt configurations.

 

Enterprise Content Connectors SAP Integration Suite provides the integration layer for connecting to external content repositories including Microsoft SharePoint, Microsoft 365, shared folders, and other enterprise document sources. Connectors extract document content and metadata. This includes file type, author, last modified date, source system, and access permissions for ingestion into the pipeline.

Document Ingestion and Chunking Pipeline Ingested documents are pre-processed to extract clean text from PDFs, Word documents, Excel files, and PowerPoint decks. Documents are then split into semantically coherent chunks, typically 300 to 500 tokens, to ensure that embedding vectors represent focused, retrievable units of content rather than entire documents. Metadata is extracted and associated with each chunk, including document title, source system, last modified date, document type, and access control attributes.

Embedding Model and Vector Store Each document chunk is passed to an embedding model via the SAP Generative AI Hub. The embedding model converts the text into a high-dimensional vector that captures its semantic meaning. These vectors are stored in the SAP HANA Cloud Vector Engine.

SAP HANA Cloud's Vector Engine supports vector CRUD operations through SQL and is purpose-built for use cases including semantic search, RAG, similarity search, recommendations, and classification. A key benefit is that vector data, relational data, metadata, and access control information can all reside within the same governed platform, simplifying data architecture and security management.

Semantic Search and Relevance Ranking Layer When a user submits a query, it is converted to an embedding using the same model used during ingestion. The SAP HANA Cloud Vector Engine performs a similarity search - using cosine similarity or L2 distance - to identify the document chunks most semantically proximate to the query vector. Results are then ranked using a composite relevance score that incorporates multiple signals (described in the Implementation section below).

Security and Access Control Layer Document-level permissions from source systems are preserved throughout the pipeline. Each document chunk is tagged with its source system access control metadata. At query time, the agent filters results to return only documents the requesting user is authorised to access. SAP BTP's role-based access control and SAP Cloud Identity services provide the authentication and authorisation framework.

 Implementation Approach

Phased Development Plan

A phased approach reduces delivery risk, allows early value realisation, and enables iterative refinement of relevance quality before broad rollout.

Phase 1 – Foundation

Step 1: Identify and Prioritise Document Sources

Begin by cataloguing the enterprise content landscape. Identify which repositories contain the highest-value knowledge for the target user group. For most SAP customers, the recommended starting point is SAP support KBAs, functional design documents (FDDs), technical specifications, and process documentation. Prioritise sources where users currently experience the greatest difficulty finding relevant content.

Step 2: Define KBA Taxonomy and Metadata Standards

Establish a consistent metadata schema across all document sources. Key metadata fields should include: document type, functional area, SAP module or product, author, creation date, last modified date, source system, access classification, and version. Consistent metadata is essential for effective filtering, ranking, and governance.

Step 3: Connect to Content Repositories

Use SAP Integration Suite to establish connectors to Microsoft SharePoint, Microsoft 365, shared network folders, and other identified repositories. Configure authentication, access permissions, and incremental synchronisation schedules to ensure the index remains current as documents are created or updated.

Phase 2 – Ingestion and Indexing (offline)

 Step 4: Ingest, Preprocess, and Chunk Documents

Extract text from all supported document formats - PDF, DOCX, XLSX, PPTX, and plain text. Apply preprocessing to remove headers, footers, and formatting artefacts. Split documents into chunks of approximately 300–500 tokens using a recursive character text splitter or equivalent approach, with a small overlap between adjacent chunks to preserve contextual continuity.

Step 5: Generate Embeddings and Store Vectors

Pass each chunk to the embedding model via the SAP Generative AI Hub. Store the resulting vectors in SAP HANA Cloud's Vector Engine alongside the associated metadata and chunk text. The SAP Cloud Application Programming Model (CAP) can serve as the application layer managing this pipeline, with native support for vector data types and integration with the SAP HANA Cloud ecosystem.

Step 6: Apply Metadata Enrichment and Document-Level Permissions

Enrich each stored chunk with its full metadata record. Associate source-system access control attributes with each chunk so that permission filtering can be applied at query time. Validate that permission inheritance from source systems (e.g., SharePoint site permissions) is correctly reflected in the index.

Phase 3 – Search, Ranking, and Pilot (online)

 Step 7: Implement Semantic Search and Relevance Scoring

Deploy the query pipeline: user query → embedding generation → vector similarity search → result retrieval. Implement a composite relevance ranking engine that combines multiple signals to produce a final ranked list of documents for each query.

Step 8: Relevance Ranking Signals

The ranking engine should incorporate the following signals:

Signal

Description

Semantic similarity

Cosine similarity score between query vector and document chunk vector

Document freshness

Recency of last modification date; more recently updated documents score higher

Source trust level

Configurable weighting by source type (e.g., official SAP KBA > internal wiki > email attachment)

Metadata match

Alignment between query context and document metadata (e.g., SAP module, document type)

Usage signals

Historical click-through and positive feedback data from prior user interactions

User context

User's role, functional area, or system context to personalise result relevance

Step 9: Test with Representative Queries and Pilot Users

Assemble a set of representative queries drawn from real user scenarios - support tickets, process questions, configuration queries. Evaluate retrieval quality by assessing whether the top-ranked results are genuinely relevant to each query. Engage a pilot user group of 10–20 users from the target functional area. Collect structured feedback on result relevance and usability. Iterate on chunking strategy, metadata weighting, and ranking logic based on findings before broader rollout.

Recommendations

Practical Guidance for SAP Customers

  1. Establish Data Readiness Before Indexing The quality of search results is directly dependent on the quality of the underlying content. Before indexing, assess document quality across target repositories. Remove outdated, duplicate, or superseded documents. Establish a content governance process to maintain index quality over time. Poorly governed content will produce poor search results regardless of the sophistication of the AI model.
  2. Start with a High-Value, Bounded Domain Do not attempt to index all enterprise content in the first phase. Begin with a single, high-value domain where the need for better knowledge discovery is clearly felt and measurable. Recommended starting points include:
  • SAP support KBAs and incident resolution guides
  • Functional design documents and technical specifications
  • SAP implementation project knowledge repositories
  • Process documentation for a specific SAP module (e.g., Finance, Procurement, HR)

A bounded scope enables faster delivery, clearer success measurement, and a more controlled environment for relevance tuning.

  1. Preserve and Enforce Source-Level Permissions Access control is non-negotiable. The agent must not surface documents to users who are not authorised to access them in the source system. Implement permission filtering at the retrieval layer, not as a post-processing step. Leverage SAP BTP's role-based access control and SAP Cloud Identity services to manage authentication. Regularly audit permission mappings as source system access controls change. SAP Joule is designed to be compliant with SAP product standards, AI ethics, and GDPR, providing a responsible AI foundation for the solution.
  2. Define Success Measures Before Rollout Establish clear, measurable success criteria prior to pilot launch. Recommended metrics include:
  • Retrieval precision: Percentage of top-5 results rated as relevant by users
  • Time-to-document: Reduction in average time taken to locate a relevant document
  • Support ticket deflection: Reduction in tickets raised for issues covered by indexed KBAs
  • User adoption rate: Percentage of target users actively using the agent within 60 days of launch
  1. Plan for Continuous Relevance Tuning Relevance quality degrades over time if the index is not maintained. Establish operational processes for: incremental document ingestion as new content is created; periodic re-indexing of modified documents; review and adjustment of ranking weights based on usage signal data; and regular user feedback collection. The SAP AI Launchpad provides monitoring and management capabilities to support ongoing model and pipeline oversight.

6. Adopt a Responsible AI Posture RAG architectures reduce the risk of LLM hallucination by grounding responses in retrieved documents rather than model-generated content. However, the agent should always surface source references alongside results, enabling users to verify the origin and authority of retrieved content. Implement confidence thresholds: if retrieved content is not sufficiently relevant to a query, the agent should indicate this rather than returning low-quality results.

7. Key Architectural Components The solution follows a two-core action model: an offline ingestion and indexing pipeline that processes, chunks, embeds, and stores enterprise documents; and an online query and retrieval pipeline that converts user queries to vectors, performs similarity search, applies access control filtering, and returns ranked results.

Layer

Component

Technology

User Interaction

Conversational search interface

SAP Joule / SAP Build Apps

Agent Orchestration

Application and domain logic, RAG pipeline coordination

SAP Cloud Application Programming Model (CAP)

AI Development

Pro-code agent construction, type-safe LLM integration

SAP Cloud SDK for AI

AI Services

Embedding model access, LLM access, prompt management, orchestration

SAP Generative AI Hub (via SAP AI Core)

AI Management

Model lifecycle, deployment monitoring, configuration

SAP AI Launchpad

Vector Store

Vector CRUD operations, cosine similarity / L2 distance search, metadata storage

SAP HANA Cloud Vector Engine

Knowledge Graph

Semantic relationship modelling, ontology-based reasoning, business context enrichment

SAP HANA Cloud Knowledge Graph Engine

Content Connectors

Integration to SharePoint, Microsoft 365, shared folders, document repositories

SAP Integration Suite

Document Ingestion

Text extraction from PDF, DOCX, XLSX, PPTX; chunking; metadata extraction

CAP pipeline / SAP BTP Object Store

Security & Access Control

Role-based access control, authentication, source-level permission filtering

SAP BTP Authorization & Trust Management / SAP Cloud Identity

Connectivity

Secure on-premise and cloud system connectivity

SAP Connectivity Service / SAP Destination Service

Runtime

Application hosting

SAP BTP Cloud Foundry or Kyma runtime

Other Key Architectural Considerations

Security and Access Control

  • Document-level permissions from source systems (e.g., SharePoint site permissions) must be captured during ingestion and enforced at retrieval time — not as a post-processing step.
  • SAP BTP Authorization & Trust Management and SAP Cloud Identity Services provide the authentication and authorisation framework across all layers.
  • The SAP Generative AI Hub's built-in orchestration capabilities include data masking and I/O filtering, supporting responsible AI and GDPR compliance requirements.

Semantic Search Quality

  • SAP HANA Cloud's Vector Engine natively supports semantic search, RAG, similarity search, recommendations, classifications, and anomaly detection — all within a single multi-model database, simplifying data architecture and security management.
  • Combining vector data with relational metadata, graph relationships, and spatial data within a single platform enables richer, more context-aware retrieval.
  • RAG architectures ground LLM responses in retrieved enterprise content, reducing hallucination risk. Where retrieved content is insufficiently relevant, the agent should withhold a response rather than return low-quality results.

Scalability and Performance

  • The architecture is runtime-agnostic, supporting both SAP BTP Cloud Foundry and Kyma environments.
  • SAP HANA Cloud's in-memory architecture enables real-time similarity search at enterprise scale.
  • Incremental ingestion pipelines ensure the vector index remains current as documents are created, modified, or deleted in source systems.

Content Governance and Data Readiness

  • Index quality is directly dependent on content quality. Outdated, duplicate, or superseded documents should be removed before indexing and governed continuously thereafter.
  • A consistent metadata taxonomy (document type, functional area, SAP module, access classification, version) must be defined and enforced across all source repositories before ingestion begins.
  • Starting with a bounded, high-value domain — such as SAP support KBAs, functional design documents, or process documentation for a specific SAP module — reduces delivery risk and enables measurable relevance validation before broader rollout.

Responsible AI and Observability

  • SAP AI Launchpad provides centralised monitoring of model deployments, latency metrics, and usage patterns, supporting ongoing operational oversight.
  • All results must surface source references, enabling users to verify the origin and authority of retrieved content.
  • Confidence thresholds should be implemented: if no retrieved chunk meets a minimum similarity score, the agent should indicate that no sufficiently relevant document was found rather than returning misleading results.

Conclusion

The objective of the KBA Search Agent is not to generate analytics, produce dashboards, or report on document usage. Its purpose is singular and practical: to help users find the most relevant document for their query, across all available enterprise content sources, in the least amount of time.

SAP AI solutions - including SAP AI Core, the SAP Generative AI Hub, SAP HANA Cloud's Vector Engine, SAP Joule, SAP Build, SAP BTP, and SAP Integration Suite - provide a technically credible, enterprise-grade foundation for this capability. The combination of semantic search, vector embeddings, RAG, and composite relevance ranking addresses the fundamental limitations of keyword-based retrieval and delivers a qualitatively different knowledge discovery experience.

For SAP customers, this is not a speculative future capability. The underlying components are available today. The path to value is a phased, governed implementation that starts with a high-value content domain, establishes strong data and permission foundations, and iterates toward broader coverage based on demonstrated user value.

Enterprise knowledge exists. The challenge is making it findable. The KBA Search Agent, built on SAP AI solutions, is a practical and scalable answer to that challenge.

ATUL Architecture #6 — Intelligent Utility Blueprint: End‑to‑End Architecture on SAP BTP

Executive Summary

Utilities are entering a new era where customer expectations, regulatory mandates, and operational realities demand real‑time responsiveness. This blueprint demonstrates how SAP BTP enables utilities to evolve from batch‑driven processes to intelligent, event‑driven operations. By integrating Event Mesh for reliable routing, AI Core for predictive analytics, Joule for AI reasoning, and Build Process Automation for governed workflows, utilities can achieve resilience, efficiency, and customer‑centric outcomes. The result is a self‑healing, intelligent utility enterprise that reduces risk, improves trust, and scales innovation.

Why This Matters

Utilities are under pressure to modernize. Customers expect transparency, regulators demand compliance, and operations must run in real time. Batch‑driven processes are no longer enough. The answer is an event‑driven, AI‑powered, automated utility architecture — built on SAP BTP.

The Big Picture

This blueprint shows how events, AI, and automation connect across the utility enterprise. It’s one consolidated view — the “big picture” that ties together smart meters, SAP S/4HANA Utilities, SAP BTP services, and intelligent workflows.

Reference Architecture Principles

The Intelligent Utility Blueprint is based on six architectural principles:

  • Event First Architecture
  • AI by Default
  • Cloud Native Integration
  • Zero Trust Security
  • Process Intelligence
  • API First Design

These principles ensure scalability, resilience, extensibility, and future-proof modernization.

Architecture Flow

 

Industry Drivers  

Utilities face unprecedented pressures:

  • Electrification is driving demand growth across vehicles, heating, and industry.
  • DER integration (solar, batteries, EVs) adds complexity and variability to grid operations.
  • AI data centers are emerging as massive, non‑negotiable loads.
  • Regulatory pressure demands transparency, compliance, and resilience. Together, these forces make batch‑driven processes obsolete — utilities must operate in real time.

Technology Foundation:

The SAP BTP technology stack provides the backbone for intelligent utility operations:

  • Integration Suite for enterprise connectivity.
  • AI Core for predictive models.

  • The architecture also supports SAP Clean Core principles by externalizing extensions, event processing, AI services, and automation workflows onto SAP BTP, minimizing customizations within SAP S/4HANA Utilities.

Why SAP BTP

Unlike custom-built event-driven platforms that require significant integration and operational effort, SAP BTP provides a unified foundation that combines integration, Event, AI, automation, analytics, and governance within a single business technology platform. For utilities already operating SAP landscapes, this accelerates modernization while reducing platform complexity and technical debt. By externalizing innovation onto SAP BTP, utilities can also support SAP Clean Core principles while rapidly deploying new capabilities without disrupting core business processes.

Security & Resilience

Modern utilities must withstand both cyber and climate threats:

·       Cybersecurity safeguards customer and operational data.

·       Failover and redundancy keep systems running during outages.

·       Extreme weather resilience ensures continuity during floods, heat waves, or storms. Security and resilience are embedded into every layer of architecture.

entry.title: Cloud Foundry vs Kyma: What's Under the Hood
entry.content:
SAP BTP has three main runtimes: Cloud Foundry, Kyma, and the ABAP Environment. This post covers the first two — as a dyed-in-the-wool Basis bod learning BTP, Cloud Foundry and Kyma are genuinely new ground, while the ABAP Environment feels somewhat familiar by comparison.

Most comparisons between Cloud Foundry and Kyma stop at the command level — cf push versus kubectl apply, cf bind-service versus a Kubernetes Secret. This post looks at what's actually happening underneath those commands on each platform. Cloud Foundry is an open-source platform-as-a-service, with SAP's runtime adding BTP-specific services and integrations on top of it. Kyma is a Kubernetes-based platform that adds SAP-specific extensions and integrations on top of Kubernetes.

Scheduling: Diego vs the Kubernetes control plane

Cloud Foundry's application runtime is built around Diego and Garden. Garden provides container management and isolation for application instances, while Diego handles scheduling and desired-state management — it decides which cell runs an app instance and restarts it if it dies.

Kyma has no equivalent single component. Scheduling is the Kubernetes control plane itself: kube-apiserver, the scheduler, etcd for state. In Kyma, a Deployment describes the desired state of a workload, while the Kubernetes scheduler decides where the resulting Pods actually run. Image creation and routing are separate concerns handled elsewhere. cf push does all of that (upload, stage, buildpack execution, image creation, deployment, routing) in one command; a Deployment only covers the deployment step.

Routing

Cloud Foundry uses Gorouter as its routing layer. Requests to application routes are forwarded through Gorouter to the appropriate application instance.

Kyma typically uses Istio sidecar proxies (Envoy) to participate in the service mesh, and an APIRule tells Kyma's API Gateway (also Istio-based) how to expose a service externally, including auth rules.

Service binding

For SAP BTP managed services, both platforms ultimately rely on the Open Service Broker API (OSBAPI) through BTP Service Manager. Where they differ is what happens with the result.

Cloud Foundry: cf bind-service triggers a broker, which provisions credentials that CF injects into the app's environment as VCAP_SERVICES at startup.

Kyma: the SAP BTP Operator, itself a Kubernetes controller, watches for ServiceInstance and ServiceBinding custom resources, talks to BTP's Service Manager behind the scenes — via the same OSBAPI standard — and writes the resulting credentials into a Kubernetes Secret instead of an env var.

Worked example: deploying and routing

Cloud Foundry:

cf push myapp

For a simple deployment, that's effectively the whole thing. Diego schedules it, Garden containers it, Gorouter routes it, all hidden behind one command.

Kyma needs three separate resources, applied directly. First, the namespace — for the Istio-based routing model shown here, the namespace must have sidecar injection enabled:

kubectl create namespace demo-app
kubectl label namespace demo-app istio-injection=enabled

Then the Deployment, Service, and APIRule together:

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: hello-kyma
  namespace: demo-app
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: hello-kyma
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: hello-kyma
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: hello
        image: hashicorp/http-echo:latest
        args:
          - "-text=Hello from Kyma!"
        ports:
        - containerPort: 5678
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: hello-kyma-service
  namespace: demo-app
spec:
  selector:
    app: hello-kyma
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 5678
---
apiVersion: gateway.kyma-project.io/v2
kind: APIRule
metadata:
  name: hello-kyma-api
  namespace: demo-app
spec:
  gateway: kyma-system/kyma-gateway
  hosts:
    - hello-kyma.c-xxxxx.kyma.ondemand.com
  service:
    name: hello-kyma-service
    port: 80
  rules:
    - path: /*
      methods: ["GET"]
      noAuth: true
kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml
kubectl get pods -n demo-app -w

Watch for 2/2 in the pod's container count — that's the app container plus the Istio sidecar together. One container running means the sidecar never attached, usually because the namespace label above is missing.

curl https://hello-kyma.c-xxxxx.kyma.ondemand.com

Worked example: service binding

Cloud Foundry:

cf create-service xsuaa application myxsuaa
cf bind-service myapp myxsuaa

Credentials land in VCAP_SERVICES in the app's environment automatically on next restage.

In Kyma, the SAP BTP Operator handles this via ServiceInstance and ServiceBinding custom resources instead of CLI commands. The binding produces a Kubernetes Secret, which the app reads by mounting it as a volume or environment variable in its own Deployment spec, rather than anything being injected automatically.

Opinionated versus composable

The Diego/Garden versus Kubernetes control plane split matters, but it's not the biggest difference between the two day to day. That's really about how much the platform decides for you.

Cloud Foundry is opinionated:

Source code
    ↓
cf push
    ↓
Buildpack
    ↓
Container
    ↓
Route

Kyma is composable:

Container image
    ↓
Deployment
    ↓
Service
    ↓
APIRule
    ↓
Gateway

Cloud Foundry gives you a paved road. Kyma gives you Kubernetes primitives and expects you to wire them together yourself.

Why SAP keeps both

Cloud Foundry is the mature, established runtime — it still forms the backbone for many existing SAP and partner extensions. Kyma is built around Kubernetes, aligned with where the broader industry has settled. SAP's position is not that one replaces the other: Cloud Foundry remains the runtime for existing applications and extensions, while Kyma targets Kubernetes-native, event-driven, and more composable scenarios.

Implications for learners

There's one particularly thorny issue for learners: getting access to the runtimes in the first place. SAP restricted CF deployment in Nov 2025 for trial accounts. Unfortunately, Kyma runtime has also been discontinued for trial accounts, and its Free Tier plan is capped at just 30 days, usable once per account — practically unavailable unless you're on a full, paid subscription.
