entry.title: Troubleshoot Your Cluster Directly from Kyma Dashboard with Terminal
entry.content:
Troubleshoot Your Cluster Directly from Kyma Dashboard with Terminal
Troubleshooting applications running in Kubernetes often requires switching between tools, creating temporary resources, and preparing the environment before you can even start investigating the actual problem.
 
To simplify this experience, Kyma dashboard (Busola) will introduce a new Terminal feature on October 6, 2026. It will provide direct, browser-based access to your cluster and include common troubleshooting tools such as curl, jq, and yq, allowing you to start debugging immediately without creating temporary workloads or installing additional utilities.
 
Why We Built It
If you've worked with Kubernetes applications, you've probably encountered situations where you needed to verify connectivity, inspect service configuration, or debug networking issues between workloads.

A common workflow is to create a temporary Pod, install debugging tools, and only then start investigating the issue. While this approach works, it adds extra steps before troubleshooting can begin.

With the new Terminal feature, you can execute commands directly from within the cluster and focus on solving the problem instead of preparing the environment.

A Practical Example
Let's walk through a common troubleshooting scenario in Kubernetes: a Service that appears to be running correctly but is not reachable.
We'll deploy a simple Pod and Service, use the built-in Terminal to verify connectivity, identify the root cause, and validate the fix directly from Kyma dashboard.

Step 1: Create Test Resources
In Kyma dashboard, choose Upload YAML and apply the following configuration:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: my-test-env
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  namespace: my-test-env
  name: nginx
  labels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: my-api
spec:
  containers:
  - name: nginx
    image: nginx
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-service
  namespace: my-test-env
spec:
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: my-nginx
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 80
This creates:
a namespace called
  • my-test-env
  • an nginx Pod
  • a Service intended to expose the Pod
 
Step 2: Navigate to the Namespace and Check the Pod Status
Open the command palette: (macOS: Cmd + K, Windows/Linux: Ctrl + K), type ns/my-test-env, and press Enter.
To navigate to your nginx Pod open the command palette and type pods/nginx. Press Enter.
If the Pod status shows Running, your application is up.

Step 3: Verify Pod Connectivity
From the Pod details page, note the Pod IP address shown in the Status card.
Open the Terminal and run:
curl -I ${YOUR_POD_IP}
You should receive a response containing HTTP/1.1 200 OK.
This confirms that the Pod itself is reachable and serving requests.

Step 4: Test the Service
Now let's verify whether the Service is correctly configured.
Open the command palette and navigate to svc/my-service

You can call Kubernetes Services either through their ClusterIP or their DNS name. For real applications, it's recommended to use the DNS name, and this is how we proceed in this example.
Open the Terminal and execute:
curl -I my-service.my-test-env.svc.cluster.local
Instead of a successful response, you'll receive a connection error.
At first glance, this might look like a networking problem. However, the Pod itself was reachable in the previous step. Thanks to the built-in Terminal, we were able to quickly verify Pod connectivity and narrow the scope of the problem to the communication between the Service and its target Pods.

Finding the Root Cause
Looking closer at the Service configuration, the issue becomes clear.
The Pod has the label:
app.kubernetes.io/name: my-api
But the Service selector expects:
app.kubernetes.io/name: my-nginx
Because the labels don't match, the Service cannot find any target Pods and therefore has no endpoints available.
This is a common Kubernetes misconfiguration and a perfect example of a problem that's easy to diagnose from the built-in Terminal.

Fixing the Service
  1. Upload the updated YAML from the Cluster Overview page.
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-service
  namespace: my-test-env
spec:
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: my-api
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 80
2. Once the Service is updated, return to the Terminal and run:

 

curl -I my-service.my-test-env.svc.cluster.local
This time, you should receive an HTTP/1.1 200 OK response.

The Service can now successfully route traffic to the Pod.

Faster Troubleshooting Out of the Box
This simple example demonstrates the value of the new Terminal feature. With a single click, you gain access to a browser-based terminal connected directly to your cluster. There's no need to create temporary Pods or install utilities manually. You can immediately start investigating problems and validating fixes.

Try It Out
The Terminal feature is designed to make troubleshooting faster, more convenient, and more accessible directly from Kyma dashboard.
Give it a try and let us know what you think. We'd love to hear how you're using the Terminal and which troubleshooting scenarios it helps you solve. Feel free to share your feedback or create an issue in the Busola repository.
And if you'd like to stay up to date with the latest Kyma features and releases, make sure to subscribe to the What's New page.

entry.title: Teched2026-XP266 -- Ship your own sandboxed AI operations agent to Kyma in two hours
entry.content:
Bring your own agent to a contained SAP Kyma sandbox with OpenRouter

Plug OpenRouter - a public LLM aggregator - into a contained sandbox with three off-the-shelf coding agents powered by free NVIDIA Nemotron models

This is a follow-up to Teched2026-XP266 | Giving an AI agent a shell — without giving away the keys to your cluster.
That post built the contained sandbox on SAP Kyma: the box is the boundary, three trust tiers, and an agent that reasons through a frontier model it never holds the key to.
Here we add a fourth tier — an external provider — and run somebody else's coding agents on a free public model, without loosening a single guarantee.

TL;DR

  • The sandbox model generalizes. "The in-cluster LLM proxy" was never special — it was just one provider. Swap in OpenRouter (a public aggregator) and the box behaves identically: one allow-listed host, nothing else.
  • Bring the model, not the key. The real OpenRouter key lives only in the gateway. Inside the box the agent carries a sentinel; the supervisor swaps it for the real key at the wire, only for a listed binary → a listed host.
  • Three off-the-shelf agents, one image, a free model. opencode, Pi, and Qwen Code — all pointed at free NVIDIA Nemotron models on OpenRouter.
  • Containment holds with a public host in the mix. The box reaches openrouter.ai and nothing else — not the internet at large, not the API server. We prove it with three curls.
  • "External" isn't "less contained." Opening one host for named binaries, with the key injected at the wire, is a different tier — not a looser one.
  • The abstraction was the product. The sandbox never cared whether the model was in-cluster or across the planet; "provider" is the seam, and it holds.
  • A free model is a confident junior. Great for a first draft, wrong about anything niche — so make the cluster the reviewer, not the reader.

Contents

  • ⚖️ The itch
  • 🧭 The fourth tier
  • 👀 See it first
  • 🧩 How it works — profile → provider → sandbox
  • 🔍 The deep dive
    • 3a. The profile is the policy
    • 3b. The provider holds the key
    • 3c. The sandbox gets a sentinel
    • 3d. Picking a free model
  • ️🛡️ Still contained — with a public host in the mix
  • 🎯 Why it's worth it
  • 🧰 Reusable patterns
  • 📎 Appendix
  • 📚 References & BOM
  • 📖 Lexicon
  • 🎓 See it live — SAP TechEd 2026 (XP266)

⚖️ The itch — one more model, one more key

👉The first post left the agent talking to SAP AI Core, in-cluster, through an in-cluster LLM proxy — no key in the box, no route to the internet.

👉However, sooner or later someone will need a feature the in-cluster proxy doesn't bridge yet, for instance:

  • a public aggregator,
  • a shiny free model to prototype with,
  • an off-the-shelf coding agent that only knows how to talk to OpenRouter.

👉So the question remains:

How do you let an agent use an external model — reached over the public internet — without putting the key in the box or opening a route it can abuse?

👉The answer turns out to be not a new mechanism at all.

🧭 The fourth tier — an external provider

The first post had three tiers — the same sandbox image, with each tier granting a bit more access - the more you trust the workload. 

TierReachesClusterLLM Key in sandbox
1. Containedthe in-cluster LLM onlynonenone (sentinel)
2. Scoped-ops+ API server (read-only)read-only kubectlnone (sentinel)
3. Web terminalfull pod networkRBAC-scoped kubectlnone (sentinel)

This external provider adds a fourth tier — same pattern adding one more row:

TierReachesClusterLLM Key in sandbox
4. External agentone public host (openrouter.ai)nonenone (sentinel)

👉And it is not a weaker tier — it's a different one.

  • The box still can't reach the API server or the rest of the internet. 
  • And the only thing that changed is which single endpoint the supervisor opens, and that the credential behind it is a real OpenRouter key — held, as always, by the gateway and never by the box.

👀 See it first — from the web terminal

  • Kyma web terminal embeds the openshell CLI
  • the terminal runs inside the cluster, thus, you reach the gateway's Service directly (no HTTPS host, no port-forward).
  • The openshell gateway is OIDC-gated; it validates your Keycloak token itself.
  • The terminal has no browser, so you log in with the device-code flow:

 

export XP266_CLUSTER=xp266-NNN          # your runtime number
export XP266_DOMAIN=<workshop-domain>   # handed out at the session

OPENSHELL_NO_BROWSER=1 openshell gateway add http://openshell.openshell.svc.cluster.local:8080 \
  --oidc-issuer https://keycloak.$XP266_CLUSTER.$XP266_DOMAIN/realms/ateam-isveng \
  --oidc-client-id openshell-oidc
#   To authenticate, visit:
#     https://keycloak.<cluster>.<domain>/realms/ateam-isveng/device?user_code=XXXX-XXXX
#   ✓ Authenticated via device code      ← approve on your laptop, you need the `openshell-admin` role

👉pick a current free model and create the sandbox:

 

export FREE_MODEL=nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free   # a current :free NVIDIA model

openshell sandbox create --name agents \
  --from localhost:32137/openrouter-agents:latest \
  --provider openrouter \
  --env OPENAI_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 \
  --env OPENAI_MODEL=$FREE_MODEL \
  --detach -- sleep infinity &
openshell sandbox list        # wait for PHASE=Ready
👉--provider openrouter is the whole trick: it opens egress to openrouter.ai (+ models.dev) for the agent binaries only, and injects the key sentinel.

👉Run any of the three agents — same box, same model:

# opencode (open-source Bun agent):
openshell sandbox exec --name agents -- opencode run -m openrouter/$FREE_MODEL "Reply with one word: PONG"
#   PONG

# Pi (@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent):
openshell sandbox exec --name agents -- pi -p --model openrouter/$FREE_MODEL "List 3 facts about Kyma."

# Qwen Code (OpenAI-compatible — takes no -m; reads $OPENAI_MODEL):
openshell sandbox exec --name agents -- qwen -p "List 3 facts about Kyma."
 

👉An off-the-shelf coding agent just reasoned through a frontier-grade free model.

Now the punchline: try to break out

openshell sandbox exec --name agents -- sh -c '
  curl -sS -m8 -o /dev/null -w "openrouter.ai: %{http_code}\n" https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models
  curl -sS -m8 https://example.com            >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "example.com: REACHED" || echo "example.com: blocked"
  curl -sS -m8 https://kubernetes.default.svc >/dev/null 2>&1 && echo "apiserver: REACHED"   || echo "apiserver: blocked"
  echo "key in box: $OPENROUTER_API_KEY"
 
openrouter.ai: 200
example.com: blocked                     ← the rest of the internet: no route
apiserver: blocked                       ← the cluster API: no route
key in box: openshell:resolve:env:…      ← a sentinel, NOT the real key

👉One host reachable.

  • ✅Everything else refused.
  • ✅The key never in the box.
  • ✅That's the fourth tier in three curl lines.

🧩 How it works — profile → provider → sandbox

Three concepts, one key that never leaves the gateway:

  • Profile — a reusable spec, no secret in it: which credential env var, which auth style, which endpoints egress may reach, and which binaries are allowed to use the credential.
  • Provider — a profile bound to a real key. The key (sk-or-…) is stored only in the gateway.
  • Sandbox — --provider openrouter attaches it: the box receives a sentinel (not the key) + scoped egress; the supervisor swaps the sentinel for the real key at the wire, only for a listed binary reaching a listed endpoint.
 

 

Same picture, in ASCII, for renderers that don't do Mermaid:

   ┌───────────────── OpenShell gateway (holds the real key) ───────────────── ┐
   │ profile "openrouter"   credential: OPENROUTER_API_KEY (bearer)            │
   │                        endpoints : openrouter.ai, models.dev  ← only hosts│
   │                        binaries  : node, opencode, qwen, pi   ← only these│
   │ provider "openrouter" = profile + REAL KEY           ← key lives ONLY here│
   └───────────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┘
                 sandbox create --provider openrouter
                                        ▼
   ┌──────────────────── your sandbox (the box) ────────────────────┐
   │ OPENROUTER_API_KEY = openshell:resolve:…   ← a SENTINEL        │
   │ agent  ──▶  Authorization: Bearer <sentinel>                   │
   └───────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┘
                                        ▼ (allowed binary + allowed host)
            supervisor swaps  <sentinel> → sk-or-…  AT THE WIRE
                                        ▼
                                  openrouter.ai   (sees the real key; the box never did)
 
In a nutshell:
  • 👉The gateway is the keeper of secrets
  • 👉the profile is the policy
  • 👉the sentinel is what the agent gets instead of a key.

🔍 The deep dive

3a. The profile is the policy (endpoints × binaries)

  • A profile answers two questions and nothing else: which hosts may this credential reach, and which binaries may send that traffic.
  • For OpenRouter that's openrouter.ai (the inference API) plus models.dev (opencode's model-registry metadata, dialed on startup), and the agent binaries (node, opencode, qwen, pi).
  • Everything outside that cross product is denied by default — a block-list would be a guessing game; an allow-list is a decision you can read.

3b. The provider holds the key — once, in one place

  • The provider is the profile plus a real key.
  • On OpenShell 0.1.1 the key is injected into the box as a resolve-sentinel (openshell:resolve:env:…); the supervisor resolves it to the real sk-or-… only at egress, and only for an allowed binary → an allowed host.
  • The two env vars the agents read — OPENROUTER_API_KEY (Pi, opencode) and OPENAI_API_KEY (the OpenAI-compatible Qwen Code) — both carry the sentinel.
  • Compromise the agent and all you've got is the string openshell:resolve:env:….

3c. The sandbox gets a sentinel, never the secret

  • This is the same credential-injection trick from the first post, now across a public hop instead of an in-cluster one.
  • The box's view of the world: an env var that looks like a key but isn't, and exactly one host it's allowed to send it to.
  • The agent can't tell the difference — it sets Authorization: Bearer <sentinel> and the reply comes back — but an attacker who owns the agent gets a placeholder and a single, logged, allow-listed destination.

3d. Picking a free model

OpenRouter's :free tier includes NVIDIA's Nemotron family — frontier-grade, no quota spent.

  • The agents call tools, so the model must be a chat/completion model with tool-calling. Embedding/rerank models (ids with -embed- / -rerank-) are RAG parts, not chat — the agent will error.
  • Two known-good picks: nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b:free (large, higher quality) and nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning:free (smaller, faster).

🛡️ Still contained — with a public host in the mix

  • 👉 The instinct is that "the box can now reach the internet" must mean "the box is less safe."
  • 👉 It doesn't — because the internet was never opened.

Here's what each familiar threat runs into:

ThreatWhat usually enables itWhat this tier does instead
Data exfiltrationthe agent has the internetone host resolves (openrouter.ai); example.com and everything else → no route
Reaching the clusterpod → API server pathno route to kubernetes.default.svc — this tier grants no cluster access at all
Credential theftthe agent holds the keythe key is never in the box — a sentinel in, the real sk-or-… injected at the last hop
A rogue binary phoning homeany process can egressegress is binary-scoped — only node/opencode/qwen/pi may send; anything else is denied
Silent abuseno audit trailevery denied request is logged at the supervisor

 

 

🎯 Why it's worth it

You can say yes to a much wider set of "can the agent use this model?" questions, because "use" now happens somewhere it can't hurt you — even when the model lives on the public internet behind a paid key:

  • ✅ off-the-shelf coding agents (opencode, Pi, Qwen Code) you didn't write and don't fully trust, run safely
  • ✅ free models for prototyping and workshops — no quota, no standing credential in the box
  • ✅ the same contained guarantees as the in-cluster tier: one host, no cluster, key in the gateway
  • ✅ a clean generalization — "provider" means any governed endpoint, in-cluster or external, by the same rules

All on the stock OpenShell chart and agent-sandbox controller, on a normal managed Kyma cluster.

🧰 Reusable patterns

Strip out OpenRouter and several of these stand on their own — a toolkit for governing any external dependency a semi-trusted workload needs.

  • Model the credential as a profile, not an env var. Separate the spec (which hosts, which binaries, which auth) from the secret. The spec is reviewable in Git; the secret lives in exactly one guarded place. ✅ You can audit "what can reach the internet" without ever seeing a key.
  •  Scope egress by binary, not just by host. "node and opencode may reach openrouter.ai" is a far tighter statement than "the pod may reach openrouter.ai." A rogue process in the box still can't send. ✅ Lateral egress inside the box is closed, not just lateral network.
  • Inject credentials at the wire — even across a public hop. The workload carries a sentinel; the proxy swaps in the real value on the last hop out. Works identically whether the destination is in-cluster or on the internet. ✅ Compromise the workload and the attacker gets the word "placeholder".
  • One proxy, two shapes. OpenAI-compatible gateways (SAP AI Core, OpenRouter) look the same to a proxy — so one in-cluster exit can front both, spend-tracked, keys never leaving it. ✅ Add a provider without adding an egress path.
  • Free tiers make experimentation cheap — pin against their churn. A :free model is perfect for a workshop or a spike; its instability is the price. Keep a fallback and list-before-you-run. ✅ Zero-cost iteration, with a documented escape hatch when a model goes paid.
  • Let the platform adjudicate generated code. For anything an LLM writes against a niche API, make the API server the gate: --dry-run=server before trust. The draft→reject→fix loop is the workflow. ✅ The model's confidence stops mattering; the cluster's acceptance is the only verdict.

👉The recipe, in one line:

credential-as-profile → binary-scoped egress → sentinel-at-the-wire → one proxy, two shapes → free tier with a fallback → the cluster adjudicates generated code.

📎 Appendix

 

A. The provider profile (what --provider openrouter binds to)

Wired once per gateway (the real key is handed to the gateway here and never leaves it):

  • The profile lists the endpoints egress may reach (openrouter.ai, models.dev) and the binaries allowed to use the credential; the provider is that profile plus the real sk-or-….
  • Inside the box the agents see only the sentinel in OPENROUTER_API_KEY / OPENAI_API_KEY;
  • The supervisor resolves it at egress for an allowed binary → an allowed host.

The profile itself (imported into the gateway) — the whole policy is the endpoint × binary cross-product:

 

id: openrouter
display_name: OpenRouter
inference_capable: true
credentials:
  - name: api_key
    env_vars: [OPENROUTER_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY]   # agents read either; injected as a resolve-sentinel, swapped at egress
    auth_style: bearer
    header_name: authorization
endpoints:
  - { host: openrouter.ai, port: 443, protocol: rest, access: read-write }   # the inference API (/api/v1/…)
  - { host: models.dev,    port: 443, protocol: rest, access: read-only }    # opencode's model registry (dialed on startup)
binaries:
  - /usr/local/bin/node                                        # Pi + Qwen Code — the connecting process is node
  - /usr/local/bin/opencode                                    # opencode launcher symlink
  - /usr/local/lib/node_modules/opencode-ai/bin/opencode.exe   # opencode's RESOLVED Bun ELF (the symlink alone fails)

Why both OPENROUTER_API_KEY / OPENAI_API_KEY?

👉 Because the three agents expect the key under different env-var names, and listing both makes the gateway inject the sentinel under each — so whichever name an agent reads, it finds it:

  • OPENROUTER_API_KEY → Pi and opencode (OpenRouter-native).
  • OPENAI_API_KEY → Qwen Code, which is an OpenAI-compatible client and reads the OpenAI name.

Binding the real key turns the profile into a provider: 

The key is read from an in-cluster Secret and handed to the gateway once — it is stored only there, and every sandbox created --provider openrouter receives the sentinel, never the key.

(No tls: on the endpoints — the supervisor terminates TLS transparently and injects a CA bundle: CURL_CA_BUNDLE / NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS.)

 

B. The tools image — built in-cluster by kaniko

openrouter-agents:latest is built inside the cluster by kaniko (no CI, no registry credentials), from a Dockerfile that lives inline in a ConfigMap.

The three agents are the whole payload:

FROM node:24-bookworm-slim
# bash + CA certs for TLS to openrouter.ai; fd + ripgrep pre-installed so the agents' search tools work WITHOUT
# sandbox-blocked downloads; git for repo awareness; curl.
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
      bash ca-certificates fd-find git ripgrep curl \
 && ln -s /usr/bin/fdfind /usr/local/bin/fd && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
# Pi + Qwen Code — pure-JS, installed with --ignore-scripts (supply-chain hygiene, no postinstall):
RUN npm install -g --ignore-scripts "@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent@latest"
RUN npm install -g --ignore-scripts "@qwen-code/qwen-code@latest"
# opencode — postinstall ALLOWED so it fetches the correct glibc platform binary for this base → /usr/local/bin/opencode:
RUN npm install -g --allow-scripts=opencode-ai "opencode-ai@latest"
# OpenShell 0.1.x runs the sandbox as uid 10001: add a passwd entry so $USER/$HOME resolve + a writable home:
RUN echo 'agent:x:10001:0:agent sandbox:/home/agent:/bin/bash' >> /etc/passwd \
 && mkdir -p /home/agent /tmp/pi-agent && chmod -R 0777 /home/agent /tmp/pi-agent
WORKDIR /home/agent
ENV PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR=/tmp/pi-agent
 

C. OpenRouter vs SAP AI Core — the same shape

Why does an external provider slot in so cleanly?

  • Because OpenRouter and SAP AI Core are the same shape to a proxy: an OpenAI-compatible gateway behind one credential.
  • OpenRouter is a public aggregator (one endpoint, many upstreams — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Qwen, NVIDIA…)
  • SAP AI Core is SAP's managed inference gateway, reached in-cluster through a proxy.

So OpenRouter is just another provider — no new integration, the same sentinel-at-the-wire mechanism.

 SAP AI Core (via in-cluster LLM proxy)OpenRouter (via direct path)
Pathagent → in-cluster proxy → SAP AI Coreagent → OpenRouter (one allow-listed external host)
Key in boxnone — a sentinel (real key in the gateway)none — a sentinel (real key in the gateway)
Internetnoneone host: openrouter.ai

In summary:

  • 👉The key story is identical — in both, the real credential lives only in the gateway and the box carries a sentinel.
  • 👉The only things that differ are the egress path (an in-cluster service vs one public host) and whether any internet is opened at all.
  • ⚠️The one thing that does not work: OpenRouter cannot call SAP AI Core. OpenRouter only routes to its own public upstreams — it can't reach an in-cluster proxy.

📚References & BOM

The exact versions this ran on a managed SAP Kyma TechEd fleet:

 

WhatPinned versionWhereNotes
NVIDIA OpenShell0.1.1 (gateway chart + CLI)github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShellApache-2.0; beta. 0.1.x retired inference.local → direct proxy dial + resolve-sentinel
agent-sandboxv0.5.5github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandboxthe controller turning a Sandbox CR into an isolated pod
OpenRouterpublic aggregatoropenrouter.aione OpenAI-compatible endpoint + one key → many upstreams
NVIDIA Nemotron (:free)rotatingopenrouter.ai/models?max_price=0&q=nvidiatool-calling chat models
opencode · Pi · Qwen Codepinned in openrouter-agents:latestopencode.ai · @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent · @qwen-code/qwen-codethree terminal coding agents, built in-cluster by kaniko into one image
Kubernetes (Gardener shoot)v1.35.7kubernetes.iothe shoot's node/control-plane version
KymaSAP-managedkyma-project.iothe runtime
KeycloakKyma-deployedkeycloak.orgOIDC provider for the gateway (device-code + PKCE)

Tutorial this follows: NVIDIA's Run Pi with OpenRouter.

Stack: NVIDIA OpenShell · agent-sandbox · SAP Kyma Runtime · Keycloak (OIDC device-code) · OpenRouter → NVIDIA Nemotron · opencode · Pi · Qwen Code · KRO.

📖 Lexicon

TermWhat it means
Provider / profileA profile is a reusable spec — which hosts egress may reach, which binaries may use a credential, which auth style. A provider is a profile bound to a real key. The key lives only in the gateway.
SentinelThe placeholder the box gets instead of the key (openshell:resolve:env:…). The supervisor swaps it for the real key at the last hop out, only for an allowed binary → an allowed host.
SupervisorThe process injected into every sandbox that owns its single exit — enforces the allow-list and injects the real key at the wire.
OpenRouterA public LLM aggregator: one OpenAI-compatible endpoint and one key, routing to many model providers.
:free modelA model OpenRouter serves at no cost. The lineup rotates; only tool-calling chat models work with agents.
Tool-callingA model's ability to emit structured calls the agent executes (run a command, read a file). Embedding/rerank models can't, so agents error on them.
Device-code flowThe browserless OIDC login: the CLI prints a URL + short code you approve on another device. Used from the web terminal, which has no browser.

entry.title: Understanding the Shared Responsibility Model on SAP BTP: Who Owns What?
entry.content:
When you move workloads to SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP), one of the first governance questions you need to answer is deceptively simple: who is responsible for what?

It's a question that often goes unanswered until something goes wrong - a security incident, a compliance gap, an outage that exposes unclear ownership. The SAP BTP Admin Guide addresses this head-on with a clearly defined Shared Responsibility Model and understanding it is foundational to operating on the platform safely and effectively.

It's Not a Two-Party Model - It's Three

Most teams think of shared responsibility as a binary: SAP handles the platform; we handle our apps. But SAP BTP involves three distinct parties:

 

What SAP Is Responsible For

As the service provider, SAP is responsible for the following areas:

  • Global Accounts and Entitlements Provisioning

SAP creates your global account and assigns the necessary entitlements so you can start using SAP BTP. During this provisioning process, SAP grants initial global account administrator rights to your designated administrator.

  • Runtimes and Services Management

SAP manages and operates the core BTP services and runtimes - including Cloud Foundry, SAP Integration Suite, and SAP Build - and keeps them updated and secure. Depending on the runtime you use, you share responsibility differently: Kyma gives you full cluster access except the SAP-managed Kyma-system namespace, while the ABAP environment lets you manage select aspects via the Landscape Portal.

 

What You Are Responsible For

As an SAP BTP customer, you’re responsible for the following areas:

  • Change Management and Operations

You establish and run effective change management processes for your applications and integrations. If you use open-source software, you must keep it updated and include vulnerability scanning in your development process.

  • Customer Data and Content

You are responsible for your data and content, which includes ensuring data privacy.

  • Application Development and Integration

You develop and operate your applications on SAP BTP. This includes creating, deploying, and integrating them with other systems.

  • Account and Environment Management

You manage your account structure, which includes organizing directories, subaccounts, and service instances. You define an account strategy based on your organization's requirements, create and configure subaccounts for your development projects, and allocate resources and services as needed.

  • Authorization and Identity Management

You manage users and assign authorizations according to your organizational and project needs. To meet these needs, use the authorization and identity management tools that SAP provides.

 

The Shared Zones: Where Collaboration Is Essential

You and SAP share responsibility for the following key areas:

  • Observability

SAP handles platform-level monitoring for all BTP services - covering health checks, troubleshooting, housekeeping, and incident management. As a customer, you're expected to leverage BTP's built-in monitoring tools, add your own checks where needed, and manage housekeeping for your own components. If an issue falls under SAP's responsibility, raise an incident through the standard SAP support process.

  • Security and Compliance

SAP treats security and compliance as a core priority on BTP. They adhere to strict industry standards across cybersecurity, operations, and privacy, and manage risks through comprehensive programs that cover cloud environments, physical facilities, events, and employees - ensuring your data is protected and regulatory requirements are met.

  • High Availability and Disaster Recovery

SAP guarantees high availability (HA) and disaster recovery (DR) for all SAP-managed BTP services through strict Service Level Agreements (SLAs), regular backups, and built-in disaster recovery mechanisms. However, customers also carry responsibility -particularly when deploying custom applications and extensions. This includes running a minimum of three instances where applicable and configuring SAP HANA Cloud with replicas to ensure resilience and for the overall HA/DR setup to work as intended.

 

Infrastructure Provider's Responsibilities

The infrastructure level is managed by either SAP or a hyperscaler, with SAP overseeing the relationship with hyperscalers. Even when using hyperscaler regions, SAP is responsible for managing this relationship. As a customer using SAP BTP, you don't have to interact directly with the hyperscalers.

The infrastructure providers operate the physical data centers that host SAP BTP regions. Their responsibilities include:

  • Set up and maintain the data centers, including servers, networking, and power supply.
  • Ensure physical and digital security to prevent unauthorized access.
  • Meet industry-grade standards for reliability and compliance.
  • Manage infrastructure operations, including software updates and patches.

 

Why This Model Matters in Practice

For Enterprise Architects and BTP administrators, the shared responsibility model is not just a governance document - it is an operational checklist. It drives decisions about:

  • Team structure: Who in your organization owns account governance? Who owns application security? Are those roles clearly defined and staffed?
  • Security controls: Are you applying SAP's security recommendations at the application and identity layer, or assuming the platform handles it all?
  • Compliance posture: Regulators will ask what you did to protect data - "SAP is responsible for the platform" will not cover application-layer gaps
  • Incident readiness: When something goes wrong, do you have the audit logs, monitoring, and runbooks to respond within your scope - or will you be scrambling to understand what you own?

 

📔Further Reading:

  • Shared Responsibility Model Between You and SAP — SAP BTP Admin Guide
  • SAP Trust Center
  • Resilience, High Availability, and Disaster Recovery

 

SAP's Customer Quality Check (CQC) services - the Security Optimization Service (SOS) and Transport Execution Analysis (TEA) - give customers a structured, expert-led way to fulfil their side of the shared responsibility model on SAP BTP. SOS surfaces misconfigured security settings across your BTP landscape with prioritized, actionable recommendations, while TEA identifies risks in how changes move through your environment. Together, they turn the abstract concept of shared responsibility into something measurable and manageable - available to customers on SAP Enterprise Support or Mission Critical Support.

  • SAP Community blog: Introducing Self-Service Booking in SAP for Me
  • Watch this short overview video
  • Explore the Services & Support FAQs
  • SAP Support Portal Continuous Quality Check & Improvement Services

 

🔗Stay connected 

Want to stay up to date on our services? Join our SAP Cloud ALM & Cross-Solution Topics community! 

🔔Stay tuned for my upcoming blogs based on Operating Model, SAP BTP Security Recommendations.

entry.title: SAP BAIP Kyma runtime 正式落地中国：扩展云原生开发能力
entry.content:
SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime 现已在中国正式上线，在本地 SAP BAIP 上提供了一个托管 Kubernetes 运行时，支持云原生应用、微服务及 SAP 扩展开发。

云原生创新能力走近中国客户

现代企业越来越需要在不增加核心系统复杂度的前提下，扩展业务应用、连接各类系统、并持续交付新的数字化能力。

SAP BAIP 在中国已提供 Cloud Foundry runtime 作为成熟的 PaaS 选项，适用于基于 buildpack 工作流的应用部署。Kyma runtime 则面向不同的需求场景。它基于开源 Kyma 项目和 Kubernetes 构建，让开发团队可以直接使用容器化工作负载、Serverless Functions 以及更广泛的 Kubernetes 生态系统——不限编程语言和框架。任何可容器化的工作负载均可在 Kyma runtime 上运行。

2026 年 6 月 2 日，SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime 在中国（华北3）率先上线，随后于 2026 年 7 月 10 日扩展至中国（上海）——通过本地 BTPEA 商业模式，在两个区域全面开放。

现已提供哪些内容？

该服务基于 BTPEA 商业模式提供，SKU 为 8016044（面向客户的 BTPEA SKU），包含以下服务计划：

服务名称服务计划名称可用数据中心
Kyma RuntimeKyma Runtime Alibaba Cloud中国（上海）— cn40
Kyma RuntimeKyma Runtime Azure中国（华北3）— cn20

客户和合作伙伴可通过 SAP Discovery Center 查看服务及其可用地区：

  • 中国（华北3）— Kyma runtime
  • 中国（上海）— Kyma runtime

中国 BTPEA 价格表中列出了 SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime 的 Standard 计费计划。

为何重要

托管、灵活的云原生应用基础平台

自建 Kubernetes 需要持续投入集群管理、版本升级、安全补丁和基础设施运维。SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime 消除了这一负担：SAP 负责底层平台的管理，客户则完全掌控自己的应用和工作负载。开发团队可以专注于构建业务能力，而不是维护基础设施。

与 Cloud Foundry runtime 相比，Kyma 提供了一种截然不同的开发模式。Cloud Foundry 通过 buildpack 对运行时进行抽象，这种方式非常适合快速部署 Java 或 Node.js 应用，但对能运行什么、如何运行有一定限制。Kyma 没有这类约束：无论使用何种语言或框架，任何容器化工作负载都可以在 Kyma 上运行，团队还可以直接使用 Kubernetes 原生工具链——包括用于打包的 Helm、自定义资源定义、精细化资源配置，以及更广泛的 CNCF 生态系统。对于构建现代云原生应用或需要精确控制工作负载的团队而言，这种灵活性是显著的优势。

两种运行时相辅相成。Cloud Foundry 仍然是 buildpack 应用部署的可靠选择；当团队需要容器原生的灵活性、多语言支持或 Kubernetes 生态工具时，Kyma 则更为适合。

通过事件驱动集成扩展 SAP 应用

Kyma runtime 内置了 Eventing 组件，允许应用直接订阅来自 SAP S/4HANA 及其他 SAP 系统的业务事件——扩展程序可以实时响应销售订单创建、货物移动或主数据变更等事件，无需轮询或点对点连接。由于该能力已集成在运行时中，团队无需单独配置消息服务即可开始构建事件驱动扩展。

结合 Serverless Functions 和内置 API Gateway，这使得构建轻量、松耦合的扩展程序变得切实可行——这些扩展与 SAP 核心系统并行运行，而非嵌入其中。自定义逻辑独立演进，升级周期解耦，核心系统保持稳定。

对于超出 SAP 间集成范畴的场景——连接第三方系统、编排多步骤工作流或构建全新业务应用——Kyma 提供了同样的 Kubernetes 基础平台，并具备灵活引入任何所需服务或技术的能力。

扩展本地 SAP BAIP 开发组合

随着 Kyma runtime 在中国（华北3）和中国（上海）相继上线，中国客户在 SAP BAIP 上多了一个可用的运行时选择。

对于正在构建容器化应用、API 集成、事件驱动扩展或微服务的团队，这一选项尤为实用。

Kyma runtime 的上线拓宽了中国生态系统可用的技术选择，为云原生应用开发提供了又一个坚实基础。

entry.title: Bringing SAP BAIP, Kyma Runtime to China: Expanding Cloud-Native Development Capabilities
entry.content:
SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime is now available in China, extending the local SAP BAIP portfolio with a managed Kubernetes-based runtime for cloud-native applications, microservices, and SAP extensions.

Bringing Cloud-Native Innovation Closer to Chinese Customers

Modern enterprises increasingly need to extend business applications, connect systems, and deliver new digital capabilities without introducing unnecessary complexity into their core landscapes.

SAP BAIP in China already offers Cloud Foundry runtime as a mature PaaS option for deploying applications using buildpack-based workflows. Kyma runtime addresses a different set of needs. Built on the open-source Kyma project and Kubernetes, it gives development teams direct access to container-based workloads, serverless functions, and the broader Kubernetes ecosystem—without restriction on programming language or framework. Any workload that can be containerized can run on Kyma runtime.

On June 2, 2026, SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime became available in China (North 3), followed by China (Shanghai) on July 10, 2026—making this managed cloud-native application runtime available through the local BTPEA commercial offering across both regions.

What Is Now Available?

SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime is offered under the BTPEA commercial model, under SKU 8016044 (the customer-facing BTPEA SKU), with the following service plans:

Service: Display NameService Plan: Display NameAvailable Data Center

Kyma RuntimeKyma Runtime AzureChina (North 3) — cn20

Customers and partners can explore the service and its regional availability through SAP Discovery Center:

  • China (North 3) — Kyma Runtime
  • China (Shanghai) — Kyma Runtime

The China BTPEA price list lists the Standard plan as a billable plan for SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime.

Why This Matters

A Managed, Flexible Foundation for Cloud-Native Applications

Running Kubernetes in-house requires ongoing investment in cluster management, upgrades, security patching, and infrastructure operations. SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime removes that burden: SAP manages the underlying platform, while customers retain full control over their applications and workloads. Development teams can focus on building business capabilities instead of maintaining infrastructure.

Compared to Cloud Foundry runtime, Kyma offers a meaningfully different development model. Cloud Foundry abstracts the runtime through buildpacks, which works well for deploying Java or Node.js applications quickly but limits what you can run and how. Kyma places no such constraints: any containerized workload runs on Kyma regardless of language or framework, and teams have direct access to Kubernetes-native tooling—Helm for packaging, custom resource definitions, fine-grained resource configuration, and the broader CNCF ecosystem. For teams building modern cloud-native applications or needing precise control over their workloads, this flexibility is a significant advantage.

The two runtimes are complementary. Cloud Foundry remains a solid choice for buildpack-based application deployment; Kyma is the better fit when container-native flexibility, polyglot development, or Kubernetes ecosystem tooling is a requirement.

Extending SAP Applications with Event-Driven Integration

Kyma runtime includes a built-in Eventing component that allows applications to subscribe directly to business events from SAP S/4HANA and other SAP systems—so an extension can react to a sales order creation, a goods movement, or a master data change in real time, without polling or point-to-point connections. Having this capability integrated into the runtime means teams can start building event-driven extensions without separately provisioning and configuring a messaging service.

Combined with serverless functions and a built-in API Gateway, this makes it practical to build lightweight, loosely coupled extensions that sit alongside the SAP core rather than inside it. Custom logic evolves independently, upgrade cycles are decoupled, and the core system remains stable.

For scenarios that go beyond SAP-to-SAP integration—connecting third-party systems, orchestrating multi-step workflows, or building net-new business applications—Kyma provides the same Kubernetes-based foundation with the flexibility to incorporate any service or technology the use case requires.

Expanding the Local SAP BAIP Development Portfolio

With Kyma runtime available in China (North 3) and China (Shanghai), customers gain an additional runtime option within the local SAP BAIP portfolio.

This is particularly relevant for teams building containerized applications, API-based integrations, event-driven extensions, and microservices that complement SAP business solutions.

The availability of Kyma runtime broadens the technology choices available to the China ecosystem and provides another foundation for cloud-native application development.
